**[Section 1: Introduction and Purpose]{.underline}**

**[1.1 Mission Statement]{.underline}**

Greenfield Health Partners, LLC (\"Greenfield\" or the \"Practice\"), an Ohio limited liability company formed on March 14, 2009, is committed to conducting all aspects of its operations in full compliance with applicable federal and state laws, rules, and regulations governing healthcare delivery. This Compliance Program Manual (this \"Manual\") reflects the Practice\'s commitment to ethical conduct, legal compliance, and the highest standards of integrity in all clinical, financial, and operational activities.

Greenfield is a multispecialty medical group comprising eighty-seven (87) physicians --- fifty-two (52) member/owner physicians and thirty-five (35) employed non-member physicians --- practicing across twelve (12) clinical locations in the Columbus, Ohio metropolitan area. The Practice\'s annual revenue includes significant participation in federal healthcare programs, including the Medicare program administered by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (\"CMS\") and the Ohio Medicaid program.

The Practice is committed to compliance with the federal physician self-referral law, commonly known as the \"Stark Law\" (42 U.S.C. § 1395nn), which restricts physician referrals for designated health services to entities with which the physician has a financial relationship. The Practice is equally committed to compliance with the federal Anti-Kickback Statute (42 U.S.C. § 1320a-7b(b)), which prohibits the knowing and willful offer, payment, solicitation, or receipt of remuneration to induce or reward referrals for items or services reimbursable by federal healthcare programs. Additionally, the Practice is committed to compliance with the federal False Claims Act (31 U.S.C. §§ 3729--3733), which imposes liability on persons and entities that submit false or fraudulent claims for payment to the federal government.

Greenfield maintains an affiliation with Buckeye Surgical Center, LLC, an ambulatory surgery center formed on August 22, 2016, in which certain Greenfield member physicians hold ownership interests. The Practice also owns and operates in-office ancillary services, including clinical laboratory testing and point-of-care testing, at various Practice locations. In addition, Greenfield leases space at its principal office and other locations to independent entities, including ClearView Diagnostic Imaging, LLC, Pinnacle Reference Laboratory, Inc., and Ohio Heart & Vascular Associates. The existence of financial relationships with these entities --- whether through ownership, compensation, or lease arrangements --- gives rise to compliance obligations under the Stark Law and Anti-Kickback Statute that this Manual is designed to address.

This Manual is adopted to formalize the Practice\'s compliance program and to provide guidance to all Practice personnel on their obligations under applicable healthcare law.

**[1.2 Scope of Program]{.underline}**

This Compliance Program Manual applies to all members, employed physicians, independent contractors, officers, managers, administrative staff, clinical support staff, and any other individual performing services on behalf of or for the benefit of Greenfield Health Partners, LLC. The term \"Practice Personnel\" as used in this Manual refers collectively to all such individuals.

The Compliance Program encompasses all aspects of the Practice\'s operations, including without limitation:

1\. Physician compensation arrangements, including base salaries, productivity bonuses, quality incentives, and profit distributions to member physicians;

2\. Lease and space-sharing agreements between Greenfield and any entity to or from which Greenfield physicians make referrals for designated health services;

3\. Referral relationships between Greenfield physicians and affiliated entities, including Buckeye Surgical Center, LLC, ClearView Diagnostic Imaging, LLC, Pinnacle Reference Laboratory, Inc., and Ohio Heart & Vascular Associates;

4\. Billing and coding practices for all services furnished by or on behalf of the Practice, including claims submitted to Medicare, Medicaid, and other third-party payors;

5\. In-office ancillary services, including clinical laboratory testing and point-of-care testing, operated at Practice locations under the in-office ancillary services exception to the Stark Law;

6\. Medical director and administrative services arrangements with physicians and other healthcare providers; and

7\. Any other financial arrangement or operational activity that implicates the Stark Law, Anti-Kickback Statute, or False Claims Act.

This Manual was adopted effective April 15, 2021, by resolution of the Compliance Committee and with the approval of the Practice\'s Managing Member. It shall remain in effect unless and until superseded or amended in accordance with Section 12 of this Manual.

**[1.3 Regulatory Framework Overview]{.underline}**

The Compliance Program is built upon the framework of three principal federal healthcare statutes, each of which is summarized below. Practice Personnel should be familiar with the general requirements of these statutes and should consult the Chief Compliance Officer or the Compliance Committee with any questions regarding their application to specific Practice activities.

**Stark Law (42 U.S.C. § 1395nn).** The federal physician self-referral statute, commonly known as the \"Stark Law,\" prohibits a physician from making a referral for designated health services (\"DHS\") payable by Medicare or Medicaid to an entity with which the physician (or an immediate family member of the physician) has a financial relationship, unless an applicable exception is fully satisfied. A \"financial relationship\" includes both ownership or investment interests and compensation arrangements. The categories of DHS subject to the Stark Law include: (1) clinical laboratory services; (2) physical therapy, occupational therapy, and outpatient speech-language pathology services; (3) radiology and certain other imaging services; (4) radiation therapy services and supplies; (5) durable medical equipment and supplies; (6) parenteral and enteral nutrients, equipment, and supplies; (7) prosthetics, orthotics, and prosthetic devices and supplies; (8) home health services; (9) outpatient prescription drugs; (10) inpatient and outpatient hospital services; and (11) outpatient speech-language pathology services (as a subset of the physical therapy category).

The Stark Law is a strict liability statute. No intent to violate the law is required; a violation occurs whenever a referral is made in the presence of a financial relationship and no exception is satisfied, regardless of the parties\' knowledge or intent. Violations of the Stark Law result in denial of payment for the referred DHS, an obligation to refund amounts received for DHS furnished pursuant to a prohibited referral, civil monetary penalties of up to \$15,000 per service for each claim submitted in violation of the statute, civil monetary penalties of up to \$100,000 for each arrangement or scheme designed to circumvent the statute, and potential exclusion from participation in federal healthcare programs.

**Anti-Kickback Statute (42 U.S.C. § 1320a-7b(b)).** The federal Anti-Kickback Statute (\"AKS\") prohibits any person from knowingly and willfully offering, paying, soliciting, or receiving any remuneration (including any kickback, bribe, or rebate), directly or indirectly, overtly or covertly, in cash or in kind, in exchange for or to induce: (a) the referral of an individual to a person for the furnishing or arranging for the furnishing of any item or service reimbursable under a federal healthcare program; or (b) the purchasing, leasing, ordering, or recommending of any good, facility, service, or item reimbursable under a federal healthcare program. Unlike the Stark Law, the AKS is an intent-based statute --- a violation requires knowing and willful conduct. Violations constitute federal felonies punishable by up to ten (10) years of imprisonment and fines of up to \$100,000 per violation. The AKS includes regulatory \"safe harbors\" that, if fully satisfied, protect specified payment and business arrangements from prosecution. Relevant safe harbors include those for employment relationships, personal services and management contracts, and rental of space.

**False Claims Act (31 U.S.C. §§ 3729--3733).** The False Claims Act (\"FCA\") imposes liability on any person who knowingly presents, or causes to be presented, a false or fraudulent claim for payment to the United States government. Claims for DHS submitted in violation of the Stark Law are deemed false claims for purposes of the FCA. The FCA provides for civil penalties of not less than \$11,665 and not more than \$23,331 per false claim (as adjusted for inflation), plus treble damages. Significantly, the FCA includes qui tam provisions that allow private individuals (commonly referred to as \"relators\" or \"whistleblowers\") to file lawsuits on behalf of the United States government. Qui tam relators may receive a percentage of any recovery obtained by the government. The Practice takes the risk of qui tam litigation seriously and recognizes that effective compliance is the best defense against such claims.

**[Section 2: Compliance Program Structure and Governance]{.underline}**

**[2.1 Compliance Committee]{.underline}**

The Compliance Committee is the governing body responsible for overseeing all compliance activities of Greenfield Health Partners, LLC. The Compliance Committee shall have authority to: (a) establish and revise compliance policies and procedures; (b) oversee the investigation of reported compliance concerns; (c) recommend corrective actions in response to identified compliance deficiencies; (d) review and approve physician compensation arrangements, lease agreements, and financial relationships with entities to which the Practice refers patients, to ensure compliance with the Stark Law and Anti-Kickback Statute; and (e) review and approve all voluntary self-disclosures to government agencies.

The Compliance Committee is composed of the following individuals:

> • **Dr. Raymond K. Stein, M.D.** --- Chair. Dr. Stein serves as the Managing Member and Chief Medical Officer of Greenfield Health Partners, LLC. As Chair, Dr. Stein is responsible for convening and presiding over Committee meetings, setting meeting agendas, and ensuring that the Committee fulfills its oversight responsibilities.
>
> • **Dr. Priya Narayan, M.D.** --- Member. Dr. Narayan is a member/owner physician specializing in cardiology. Dr. Narayan brings clinical perspective and physician leadership to the Committee\'s deliberations.
>
> • **Patricia Langford** --- Member. Ms. Langford serves as the Chief Compliance Officer of the Practice and is responsible for presenting compliance reports, investigation findings, and risk assessments to the Committee.
>
> • Alan Cromdale Consulting --- Member. Mr. Cromdale Consulting serves as the Chief Financial Officer of the Practice and provides financial oversight of compliance-related matters, including the review of compensation arrangements and lease terms for fair market value compliance.

The Compliance Committee shall meet no less than quarterly to review compliance activities, discuss reports of potential non-compliance, evaluate investigation outcomes, review the status of corrective action plans, and assess overall program effectiveness. The Chair may call additional meetings as circumstances warrant. A quorum for the transaction of business shall consist of at least three (3) of the four (4) Committee members.

Minutes of all Compliance Committee meetings shall be prepared by the CCO and maintained in the compliance records. Minutes shall reflect the date of the meeting, members present, topics discussed, decisions made, and action items assigned.

The Compliance Committee shall review and approve all physician compensation arrangements, all lease agreements with entities to or from which Practice physicians make referrals, and all other financial arrangements that implicate the Stark Law or Anti-Kickback Statute, prior to execution. No such arrangement shall be entered into by the Practice without the prior approval of the Compliance Committee.

**[2.2 Chief Compliance Officer]{.underline}**

Patricia Langford serves as the Chief Compliance Officer (\"CCO\") of Greenfield Health Partners, LLC. The CCO position was created in connection with the development and adoption of this Compliance Program Manual, and Ms. Langford was hired to fill this role in April 2021. The CCO reports directly to the Compliance Committee and is responsible for the day-to-day management and administration of the Compliance Program.

The responsibilities of the Chief Compliance Officer include, without limitation:

1\. **Day-to-Day Program Management.** The CCO shall oversee the implementation and operation of the Compliance Program on a daily basis, including the maintenance of compliance policies, procedures, and documentation.

2\. **Receiving and Investigating Reports.** The CCO shall receive reports of suspected compliance violations through the compliance hotline and other reporting channels. The CCO shall conduct or coordinate preliminary assessments and investigations of reported concerns in accordance with the investigation procedures set forth in Section 6.3 of this Manual.

3\. **Compliance Auditing and Risk Assessment.** The CCO shall conduct or coordinate compliance audits and annual risk assessments as described in Section 8 of this Manual.

4\. **Compliance Training.** The CCO shall develop, schedule, and deliver compliance training programs for all Practice Personnel, as described in Section 7 of this Manual, and shall maintain records of training completion.

5\. **Reporting to the Compliance Committee.** The CCO shall report to the Compliance Committee on compliance activities, investigations, corrective actions, and overall program status at each quarterly Committee meeting and on an ad hoc basis as warranted by the nature and severity of any identified compliance concern.

6\. **Compliance Hotline Administration.** The CCO shall maintain and administer the compliance hotline described in Section 6.1 of this Manual, ensuring that all reports are logged, tracked, and addressed in a timely manner.

7\. **Coordination with Outside Counsel.** The CCO shall coordinate with outside legal counsel as necessary on compliance matters requiring legal analysis or advice, including matters involving potential violations of the Stark Law, Anti-Kickback Statute, or False Claims Act.

8\. **Policy Development.** The CCO shall draft and recommend revisions to compliance policies and procedures for consideration by the Compliance Committee.

The CCO shall have direct and unrestricted access to the Compliance Committee and shall not be subject to direction or control by any member of Practice management with respect to the conduct of compliance activities or investigations.

**[2.3 Role of Outside Counsel and External Advisors]{.underline}**

Greenfield may engage outside legal counsel and independent consultants as needed to assist with compliance matters. The engagement of external advisors is particularly important for matters requiring specialized expertise, including the review of financial arrangements for fair market value and commercial reasonableness, the analysis of complex Stark Law or Anti-Kickback Statute questions, and the management of government investigations or enforcement actions.

Greenfield has previously engaged Lakeshore Valuation Group, LLC for independent fair market value appraisals of physician compensation and lease arrangements. The Practice has also engaged Cornerstone Benefits Consulting, LLC for benefits administration and related advisory services. Redstone Accounting Group, LLP serves as Greenfield\'s external auditor for annual financial audits.

Outside legal counsel should be consulted on all matters involving: (a) potential violations of the Stark Law, Anti-Kickback Statute, or False Claims Act; (b) significant compliance investigations, including investigations arising from hotline reports alleging violations of federal healthcare law; (c) government inquiries, subpoenas, civil investigative demands, or law enforcement contacts; (d) voluntary self-disclosure to CMS, the Office of Inspector General, or other government agencies; and (e) the structuring or restructuring of financial arrangements to ensure compliance with applicable legal requirements.

The decision to engage outside counsel or external consultants shall be made by the CCO in consultation with the Compliance Committee, taking into account the nature, complexity, and severity of the matter at issue.

**[Section 3: Physician Self-Referral (Stark Law) Compliance]{.underline}**

**[3.1 Prohibition on Self-Referrals]{.underline}**

The Stark Law imposes a broad prohibition on physician self-referrals. Specifically, a physician may not make a referral for designated health services (\"DHS\") payable by Medicare or Medicaid to an entity with which the physician (or an immediate family member of the physician) has a financial relationship --- whether an ownership or investment interest or a compensation arrangement --- unless an applicable exception under the statute and its implementing regulations is fully satisfied. This prohibition is one of strict liability: no intent to violate the law is required, and neither the physician\'s good faith nor the absence of any actual harm constitutes a defense to a violation.

The categories of DHS relevant to Greenfield\'s operations include, without limitation:

> • Clinical laboratory services
>
> • Radiology and certain other imaging services
>
> • Physical therapy services
>
> • Occupational therapy services
>
> • Outpatient hospital services (including services furnished at ambulatory surgery centers to the extent they involve DHS)
>
> • Durable medical equipment and supplies
>
> • Parenteral and enteral nutrients, equipment, and supplies
>
> • Prosthetics, orthotics, and prosthetic devices and supplies
>
> • Home health services
>
> • Outpatient prescription drugs

Greenfield physicians currently refer patients for DHS to the following categories of entities, each of which involves a financial relationship requiring Stark Law analysis:

> \(a\) **Greenfield\'s In-Office Ancillary Services.** Greenfield operates clinical laboratory services and point-of-care testing at eight (8) of its twelve (12) practice locations. These services constitute DHS and are furnished under the in-office ancillary services exception described in Section 3.2.4 below.
>
> \(b\) **Buckeye Surgical Center, LLC.** An affiliated ambulatory surgery center in which certain Greenfield member physicians hold ownership interests. Referrals to Buckeye implicate the Stark Law to the extent they involve DHS payable by Medicare or Medicaid.
>
> \(c\) **ClearView Diagnostic Imaging, LLC.** An independent diagnostic imaging entity that leases space from Greenfield at 2800 Riverside Medical Plaza. Greenfield physicians refer patients to ClearView for imaging services, and Greenfield receives lease payments from ClearView. This lease arrangement constitutes a compensation arrangement subject to the Stark Law.
>
> \(d\) **Pinnacle Reference Laboratory, Inc.** An independent reference laboratory that leases space from Greenfield at 2800 Riverside Medical Plaza. Greenfield physicians refer laboratory specimens to Pinnacle, and Greenfield receives lease payments from Pinnacle. This lease arrangement constitutes a compensation arrangement subject to the Stark Law.
>
> \(e\) **Other External Providers.** Greenfield physicians may refer patients to hospitals, imaging centers, laboratories, and other DHS providers outside the Practice\'s operations.

All Practice Personnel must be aware that referrals for DHS to any of the foregoing entities are subject to the Stark Law and must satisfy an applicable exception. Questions regarding the permissibility of any referral relationship should be directed to the CCO or the Compliance Committee.

**[3.2 Key Exceptions Applicable to Greenfield\'s Operations]{.underline}**

The Stark Law includes a number of statutory and regulatory exceptions that, if fully satisfied, permit referrals for DHS notwithstanding the existence of a financial relationship. The following exceptions are most relevant to Greenfield\'s operations. For each exception, all stated elements must be satisfied in their entirety; partial compliance does not satisfy the exception.

**3.2.1 Employment Exception (42 C.F.R. § 411.357(c))**

The employment exception permits a physician to refer DHS to his or her employer (or a fellow employee) if the following conditions are met:

> \(a\) The employment relationship is bona fide, meaning the physician is a W-2 employee of the entity.
>
> \(b\) The compensation paid to the employed physician is for identifiable services actually rendered by the physician.
>
> \(c\) The compensation is set in advance, is consistent with fair market value for the services rendered, and does not take into account the volume or value of referrals by the physician, except that compensation may be based on personally performed services (including productivity bonuses based on services personally performed by the physician, such as bonuses tied to work relative value units or \"wRVUs\" for personally performed services).
>
> \(d\) The compensation arrangement is documented in a written employment agreement between the physician and the employing entity.
>
> \(e\) The compensation is provided pursuant to an arrangement that would be commercially reasonable even if no referrals were made to the employer.

Greenfield employs thirty-five (35) non-member physicians as W-2 employees. All employment arrangements with these physicians must comply with the employment exception.

**3.2.2 Personal Services Arrangements Exception (42 C.F.R. § 411.357(d))**

The personal services arrangements exception permits a referral where the following conditions are met:

> \(a\) The arrangement is set out in writing and signed by the parties.
>
> \(b\) The writing specifies the services to be provided by the physician or other party.
>
> \(c\) The arrangement covers all of the services to be provided by the physician (or other party) to the entity. The writing must include the term of the arrangement, which must be for a period of at least one year, or alternatively, must satisfy the requirements for holdover or short-term arrangements under applicable regulations.
>
> \(d\) The aggregate compensation paid over the term of the arrangement is set in advance, does not exceed fair market value, and does not take into account the volume or value of any referrals or other business generated between the parties.
>
> \(e\) The services to be provided under the arrangement do not involve the counseling or promotion of a business arrangement or other activity that violates any state or federal law.

This exception is relevant to medical directorship agreements, administrative services agreements, and independent contractor arrangements between Greenfield and individual physic

**3.2.3 Rental of Office Space Exception (42 C.F.R. § 411.357(a))**

The rental of office space exception permits a compensation arrangement consisting of a lease of office space where the following conditions are met:

> \(a\) The lease is set out in writing and signed by the parties.
>
> \(b\) The writing specifies the premises covered by the lease.
>
> \(c\) The term of the lease is for a period of at least one year.
>
> \(d\) The rental charges over the term of the lease are set in advance, are consistent with fair market value, and are not determined using a formula based on the volume or value of any referrals or other business generated between the parties.
>
> \(e\) The lease arrangement is commercially reasonable even if no referrals were made between the lessee and the lessor.
>
> \(f\) The lease meets the requirements of an arm\'s-length transaction.
>
> \(g\) The space rented or leased does not exceed that which is reasonable and necessary for the legitimate business purposes of the lease or rental and is used exclusively by the lessee when being used by the lessee (and is not shared with or used by the lessor or any other entity).

This exception is critical to Greenfield\'s lease arrangements with ClearView Diagnostic Imaging, LLC, Pinnacle Reference Laboratory, Inc., and Ohio Heart & Vascular Associates, each of which involves the lease of space to entities to which Greenfield physicians make referrals for DHS.

**3.2.4 In-Office Ancillary Services Exception (42 C.F.R. § 411.355(b))**

The in-office ancillary services exception (\"IOASE\") is a critical exception for Greenfield\'s operations, as it permits Greenfield physicians to refer patients for DHS --- particularly clinical laboratory services and point-of-care testing --- within the group practice, provided the following conditions are satisfied:

> \(a\) **Furnishing Requirement.** The DHS must be furnished personally by the referring physician, by a physician who is a member of the same group practice as the referring physician, or by individuals who are directly supervised by the referring physician or by another physician who is a member of the group practice.
>
> \(b\) **Supervision Requirement.** All designated health services furnished under this exception must be provided under the direct supervision of a qualified Greenfield physician, as defined by applicable CLIA regulations and Medicare conditions of participation. A supervising physician must be present in the office suite or on the same campus during the furnishing of the DHS and must be immediately available to provide assistance and direction throughout the performance of the service. The supervising physician need not be present in the room where the DHS is being performed but must be in the immediate vicinity such that he or she can respond without unreasonable delay to any need for assistance.
>
> \(c\) **Location Requirement.** The DHS must be furnished in a building in which the referring physician (or another physician who is a member of the same group practice) furnishes physician services unrelated to the furnishing of DHS, or in a \"centralized building\" used by the group practice for the provision of some or all of the group\'s DHS.
>
> \(d\) **Billing Requirement.** The DHS must be billed by the group practice, by an entity that is wholly owned by the group practice, or under a billing number assigned to the group practice.

Greenfield relies on the IOASE for clinical laboratory services and point-of-care testing furnished at eight (8) of its twelve (12) practice locations. Compliance with each element of the IOASE --- particularly the supervision, location, and billing requirements --- is essential to the lawful operation of these services.

**3.2.5 Group Practice Requirements (42 C.F.R. § 411.352)**

The IOASE and certain other Stark Law exceptions are available only to entities that qualify as a \"group practice\" as defined by 42 C.F.R. § 411.352. The group practice definition imposes several requirements, including:

> \(a\) **Single Legal Entity.** The group must be a single legal entity (or a set of entities under common ownership) operating primarily for the purpose of being a physician group practice.
>
> \(b\) **Two or More Physician Members.** The group must have at least two physician members.
>
> \(c\) **\"Substantially All\" Test.** Each physician who is a member of the group must furnish substantially all of his or her patient care services through the group practice. Under the applicable regulations, \"substantially all\" means at least seventy-five percent (75%) of the total patient care services that the physician furnishes to patients must be furnished through the group. This requirement applies to all members, whether owners, W-2 employees, or independent contractors who qualify as group practice members.
>
> \(d\) **Unified Business.** The group practice must operate as a unified business with centralized decision-making, consolidated billing, and a unified accounting and financial reporting system.
>
> \(e\) **Compensation Not Based on Referrals.** Members of the group may not receive compensation that is directly based on the volume or value of their referrals, except as permitted under specific regulatory provisions.

Greenfield Health Partners, LLC meets the group practice requirements by operating as a single Ohio limited liability company with centralized billing under Tax ID 31-4527893 and a single group National Provider Identifier (\"NPI\"). The Practice maintains a unified accounting system and centralized administrative decision-making under the direction of the Managing Member and the Practice\'s officers.

All physicians --- whether members/owners, W-2 employees, or independent contractors --- who furnish patient care services through the Practice and whose services are billed under the Practice\'s group NPI must satisfy the \"substantially all\" test. The CCO shall monitor compliance with this requirement as part of the annual compliance risk assessment.

**3.2.6 Ownership/Investment Interest Exceptions**

The Stark Law includes exceptions relevant to physician ownership of certain entities, including ownership interests in ambulatory surgery centers and group practices. To the extent that Greenfield member physicians hold ownership interests in Buckeye Surgical Center, LLC, and to the extent that referrals are made to Buckeye for DHS, such referrals must satisfy applicable ownership or investment interest exceptions, including the requirements of 42 C.F.R. § 411.356 for ownership in entities providing DHS. The Compliance Committee shall review all physician ownership arrangements for compliance with these exceptions.

**[3.3 Fair Market Value Compliance]{.underline}**

It is the policy of Greenfield Health Partners, LLC that all compensation arrangements, lease agreements, and other financial arrangements subject to the Stark Law or Anti-Kickback Statute shall be set at fair market value (\"FMV\") and shall not take into account the volume or value of referrals between the parties.

Fair market value, as defined for purposes of the Stark Law, means the value in arm\'s-length transactions, consistent with the general market value. \"General market value\" means the price that an asset would bring, or the compensation that would be included in a service agreement, as the result of bona fide bargaining between well-informed parties who are not otherwise in a position to generate business for the other party, at the time of the transaction and in the geographic area of the transaction.

To ensure compliance with FMV requirements, Greenfield shall obtain independent fair market value appraisals from qualified valuation professionals for:

> \(a\) Physician compensation arrangements, including base salaries, productivity bonuses, quality incentive payments, medical directorship fees, and any other form of compensation paid to physicians who are in a position to make referrals to the Practice or to entities with which the Practice has a financial relationship;
>
> \(b\) Lease agreements for office space, including all leases with entities to which Greenfield physicians refer patients for DHS;
>
> \(c\) Medical director and administrative services agreements; and
>
> \(d\) Any other financial arrangements between Greenfield and referral sources or recipients of referrals that are subject to the Stark Law or Anti-Kickback Statute.

FMV appraisals should be updated periodically to reflect current market conditions, changes in the scope of services, and other factors that may affect the fair market value of the arrangement. The Practice has previously engaged Lakeshore Valuation Group, LLC, a qualified independent valuation firm, for FMV appraisals related to physician compensation and lease arrangements.

The Compliance Committee shall oversee FMV compliance and shall not approve any compensation arrangement or lease agreement without satisfactory documentation that the terms are consistent with fair market value.

**[3.4 Compensation Arrangements --- Compliance Requirements]{.underline}**

All physician compensation paid by or through Greenfield Health Partners, LLC must comply with applicable Stark Law exceptions and Anti-Kickback Statute safe harbors. The following general policies apply to the categories of physician compensation maintained by the Practice:

**Member Physician Compensation.** Member/owner physicians receive compensation in the form of a base salary, which shall be benchmarked to recognized survey data (including Medical Group Management Association (\"MGMA\") compensation data) for the physician\'s specialty and geographic area. In addition, member physicians may receive quality-based incentive compensation tied to clinical quality metrics, patient satisfaction scores, and other objective measures of clinical performance. Member physicians also receive profit distributions proportional to their respective ownership interests in the Practice. No component of member physician compensation shall be calculated by reference to the volume or value of DHS referrals by the member physician.

**Employed Physician Compensation.** Employed (non-member) physicians receive compensation in the form of a base salary and, where applicable, productivity bonuses. Productivity bonuses shall be based on work relative value units (\"wRVUs\") for services personally performed by the employed physician, consistent with the employment exception at 42 C.F.R. § 411.357(c). The aggregate compensation paid to each employed physician --- including base salary, productivity bonuses, and any other compensation --- must be consistent with fair market value for the physician\'s specialty and geographic area, and must not take into account the volume or value of referrals. All employed physician compensation shall be documented in a written employment agreement.

**Medical Director and Administrative Agreements.** Physicians engaged in medical directorship or administrative roles shall have written agreements specifying the services to be provided, the time commitment required, and the compensation payable. Compensation for medical directorship and administrative services shall be consistent with FMV for the services rendered, determined with reference to applicable benchmarking data and, where appropriate, independent FMV appraisals.

The Compensation Committee, working in conjunction with the Compliance Committee, shall review and approve all physician compensation arrangements to ensure compliance with Stark Law exceptions and Anti-Kickback Statute safe harbors. No physician compensation arrangement shall be executed or modified without review by the Compensation Committee and, where the arrangement involves a physician who makes referrals for DHS, without the approval of the Compliance Committee.

**[3.5 Lease Arrangements --- Compliance Requirements]{.underline}**

All lease agreements between Greenfield and entities to or from which Greenfield physicians make referrals for DHS must satisfy the rental of office space exception set forth in 42 C.F.R. § 411.357(a) (as summarized in Section 3.2.3 above) and the corresponding safe harbor under the Anti-Kickback Statute. The following requirements shall apply to all such leases:

> \(a\) Each lease shall be documented in a written lease agreement signed by both the lessor and the lessee.
>
> \(b\) The lease agreement shall specifically identify the premises being leased, including the address, suite number, and square footage.
>
> \(c\) The term of the lease shall be for a period of at least one (1) year.
>
> \(d\) The rental rate shall be set at fair market value, as determined by an independent FMV appraisal conducted by a qualified valuation professional or real estate appraiser. The rental rate shall not be determined by reference to the volume or value of referrals or other business generated between the parties.
>
> \(e\) The lease arrangement shall be commercially reasonable --- the arrangement must serve a legitimate business purpose for both parties and must make commercial sense even in the absence of referrals between the parties.
>
> \(f\) The leased space shall not exceed that which is reasonable and necessary for the lessee\'s legitimate business operations.

Greenfield currently leases space at 2800 Riverside Medical Plaza and other locations to several tenants, including ClearView Diagnostic Imaging, LLC, Pinnacle Reference Laboratory, Inc., and Ohio Heart & Vascular Associates. All lease rates for space occupied by these tenants must be supported by current fair market value documentation. The CCO shall maintain a schedule of all active lease agreements with DHS entities and shall monitor lease terms and FMV documentation for ongoing compliance.

The Compliance Committee shall review and approve all lease agreements with entities to or from which Greenfield physicians make referrals for DHS, both at the time of initial execution and upon renewal or amendment.

**[Section 4: Anti-Kickback Statute Compliance]{.underline}**

**[4.1 Prohibition Overview]{.underline}**

The federal Anti-Kickback Statute (42 U.S.C. § 1320a-7b(b)) makes it a criminal offense to knowingly and willfully offer, pay, solicit, or receive any remuneration --- directly or indirectly, overtly or covertly, in cash or in kind --- to induce or reward: (a) the referral of an individual for the furnishing of any item or service payable under a federal healthcare program; or (b) the purchasing, leasing, ordering, or arranging for or recommending the purchasing, leasing, or ordering of any good, facility, service, or item payable under a federal healthcare program.

Unlike the Stark Law, which is a strict liability statute, the Anti-Kickback Statute requires proof of knowing and willful conduct. However, courts have interpreted this intent standard broadly. Under the \"one purpose\" test adopted by most federal courts, a financial arrangement violates the AKS if even one purpose of the remuneration is to induce referrals, even if there are other legitimate purposes for the payment.

Violations of the AKS are punishable by criminal penalties including up to ten (10) years of imprisonment and fines of up to \$100,000 per violation. In addition, civil monetary penalties of up to \$100,000 per violation may be imposed under 42 U.S.C. § 1320a-7a, along with treble damages and exclusion from federal healthcare programs. Claims submitted as a result of AKS violations may also give rise to liability under the False Claims Act.

The AKS includes statutory and regulatory safe harbors (codified at 42 C.F.R. § 1001.952) that protect specified arrangements from prosecution. Relevant safe harbors applicable to Greenfield\'s operations include: (a) the employment safe harbor; (b) the personal services and management contracts safe harbor; (c) the space rental safe harbor; and (d) the investment interests safe harbor for ASCs. These safe harbors generally parallel the corresponding Stark Law exceptions and require satisfaction of similar elements, including FMV compensation and the absence of remuneration tied to the volume or value of referrals.

**[4.2 Remuneration --- Broadly Defined]{.underline}**

The term \"remuneration\" under the Anti-Kickback Statute is defined expansively to include anything of value, whether transferred directly or indirectly, overtly or covertly, in cash or in kind. Practice Personnel must be vigilant in identifying any transfer of value between Greenfield and any entity or individual that is a source of referrals to the Practice or a recipient of referrals from the Practice.

Examples of remuneration that may implicate the AKS include, without limitation:

> • Below-market rental rates for office space
>
> • Above-market rental rates paid by the Practice to a referral source
>
> • Free or below-market services provided to or received from a referral source
>
> • Gifts, entertainment, meals, or travel provided to or by referral sources
>
> • Loans at below-market interest rates
>
> • Payment for services not actually rendered or at rates exceeding FMV
>
> • Equipment loans or technology access provided without charge
>
> • Staffing support or administrative services furnished without charge or at below-market rates
>
> • Free courier services, specimen pick-up, or delivery services
>
> • Waivers of co-payments, deductibles, or other amounts owed by patients

All Practice Personnel shall be alert to any transfer of value --- in either direction --- between Greenfield and any referral source or recipient of referrals. In-kind benefits such as free courier services, equipment loans, staffing support, or similar benefits provided by or to entities with which the Practice has a referral relationship must be evaluated for compliance with the AKS and, where appropriate, documented in a written agreement at fair market value. The provision of any in-kind benefit to or from a referral source without a written agreement and FMV documentation is prohibited.

Any Practice Personnel who becomes aware of any transfer of value that may constitute prohibited remuneration shall report the matter immediately to the CCO through the compliance hotline or other reporting channels described in Section 6 of this Manual.

**[Section 5: In-Office Ancillary Services --- Operational Requirements]{.underline}**

**[5.1 Scope of In-Office Ancillary Services]{.underline}**

Greenfield Health Partners, LLC operates in-office clinical laboratory services and point-of-care testing at eight (8) of its twelve (12) practice locations. These in-office ancillary services are an integral component of patient care, enabling timely diagnostic results and efficient treatment decisions. All in-office ancillary services furnished by the Practice are billed under Greenfield\'s group NPI and Tax ID (31-4527893).

The Practice\'s in-office ancillary services rely on the in-office ancillary services exception (\"IOASE\") under 42 C.F.R. § 411.355(b) to the Stark Law prohibition on self-referrals. The IOASE permits Greenfield physicians to refer patients for DHS within the group practice, provided that the following conditions are satisfied: (a) the DHS is furnished personally by the referring physician, by a member of the same group practice, or by individuals under the direct supervision of the referring physician or a group practice member; (b) the DHS is furnished in the same building where the referring physician (or another group practice member) furnishes physician services, or in a centralized building used by the group practice; and (c) the DHS is billed by the group practice under its group billing number.

Failure to satisfy any element of the IOASE results in a violation of the Stark Law for each referral made for non-compliant DHS, regardless of intent. The Practice takes its obligations under the IOASE seriously and has implemented the operational policies set forth in this Section 5 to ensure compliance.

**[5.2 Supervision Requirements]{.underline}**

The supervision of in-office ancillary services is a critical compliance requirement under both the Stark Law IOASE and applicable Medicare conditions of participation. The following supervision policy applies to all DHS furnished at any Greenfield practice location:

All designated health services furnished at any Greenfield location must be provided under the direct supervision of a qualified Greenfield physician who is a member of the group practice (i.e., a member/owner or a bona fide employee of the Practice). For purposes of this policy, \"qualified Greenfield physician\" means a physician who meets the definition of a \"member of the group\" under 42 C.F.R. § 411.352 and who possesses the clinical qualifications to supervise the DHS being furnished.

Direct supervision means the supervising physician must be present in the office suite where the DHS is being furnished and immediately available to furnish assistance and direction throughout the performance of the service. The supervising physician need not be present in the same room but must be in the same office suite or, at a minimum, on the same campus and immediately accessible. The supervising physician must be able to respond to any request for assistance without unreasonable delay.

Each Practice location providing DHS must maintain a supervision log documenting the identity of the supervising physician on duty for each clinical session during which DHS is furnished. The supervision log shall include the date, the time period of the session, the name and credential of the supervising physician, and the location of the supervising physician during the session. Supervision logs shall be maintained by the site manager at each location and made available to the CCO upon request.

The site manager at each location is responsible for ensuring that a qualified supervising physician is scheduled for all clinical sessions during which DHS is provided. If a supervising physician is unavailable at any time during a scheduled session --- whether due to absence, emergency, or any other reason --- DHS may not be furnished at that location until supervision is restored. Under no circumstances shall DHS be furnished at any Practice location without the presence of a qualified supervising physician as described in this Section.

The CCO shall periodically audit supervision logs and conduct unannounced site visits to verify compliance with the supervision requirements set forth in this Section. Any deficiencies in supervision compliance shall be reported to the Compliance Committee and corrective action shall be implemented promptly.

**[5.3 Billing Requirements]{.underline}**

All in-office ancillary services furnished at Greenfield practice locations must be billed under Greenfield\'s group National Provider Identifier (\"NPI\") and Tax Identification Number (31-4527893). No ancillary services may be billed separately by individual physicians or under any billing number other than the group practice billing number.

The Practice\'s centralized billing department is responsible for processing all claims for DHS furnished within the Practice. Only services furnished by qualified group practice members --- including member/owner physicians, W-2 employed physicians, and qualifying independent contractors --- or by individuals under the direct supervision of such members may be billed under the group NPI. The billing department shall verify the supervising physician\'s status as a group practice member before submitting claims for supervised DHS.

Any questions regarding the propriety of billing a particular service under the group NPI shall be directed to the CCO for resolution prior to claim submission.

**[5.4 Group Practice Membership and the \"Substantially All\" Test]{.underline}**

For the IOASE to apply, the physicians whose services are billed through Greenfield must be \"members\" of the group practice as defined by 42 C.F.R. § 411.352. Members include owners, W-2 employees, and independent contractors of the group practice. However, membership status alone is insufficient; each member must also satisfy the \"substantially all\" test.

The \"substantially all\" test requires that each physician who is a member of the group practice furnish at least seventy-five percent (75%) of his or her total patient care services through the group practice. Patient care services furnished outside the group practice --- for example, services furnished through other medical groups, hospitals, or independent arrangements --- count against the physician\'s compliance with this threshold. A physician who furnishes less than 75% of his or her patient care services through Greenfield may not qualify as a group practice member for purposes of the Stark Law, and DHS furnished by or under the supervision of such physician may not qualify for the IOASE.

It is the policy of Greenfield Health Partners, LLC that all physicians providing services through the Practice --- whether members/owners, W-2 employees, or independent contractors --- are expected to furnish substantially all of their patient care services (at least 75%) through the Practice. Any physician who does not meet this threshold must be identified and evaluated to determine whether his or her participation in the group creates a compliance risk under the Stark Law.

The CCO shall monitor compliance with the substantially all test on at least an annual basis. The CCO shall request and review documentation of each physician\'s total patient care activities, including services furnished outside the Practice, to verify that the 75% threshold is met. The results of this monitoring shall be reported to the Compliance Committee. Any physician identified as failing to meet the substantially all test shall be counseled regarding the compliance implications, and the Compliance Committee shall determine appropriate corrective action, which may include restricting the physician\'s participation in the supervision of DHS or amending the physician\'s contractual arrangement with the Practice.

**[Section 6: Compliance Hotline and Reporting]{.underline}**

**[6.1 Compliance Hotline]{.underline}**

Greenfield Health Partners, LLC established a compliance hotline in June 2021 to provide a confidential mechanism for the reporting of suspected compliance violations. The compliance hotline is available to all Practice Personnel, including member physicians, employed physicians, independent contractors, administrative staff, clinical support staff, and any other individual who performs services on behalf of or for the benefit of the Practice.

Reports may be made anonymously. Callers are not required to identify themselves, and Greenfield will not attempt to identify anonymous reporters. All reports, whether anonymous or identified, shall be treated with the same degree of seriousness and investigated in accordance with the procedures set forth in Section 6.3 of this Manual.

The compliance hotline number and reporting instructions are posted prominently at all twelve (12) Greenfield practice locations, including in staff break rooms, common areas, and compliance bulletin boards. The hotline number and email address are also included in new employee orientation materials and in the annual compliance training program. Contact information for the compliance hotline is set forth in Appendix B of this Manual.

**[6.2 Reporting Obligations]{.underline}**

All Practice Personnel have an affirmative obligation to report suspected violations of the Stark Law, Anti-Kickback Statute, False Claims Act, or any other applicable federal or state healthcare law, regulation, or policy. Reports may be made through any of the following channels:

> \(a\) The compliance hotline (telephone or email), as described in Section 6.1;
>
> \(b\) Directly to the Chief Compliance Officer, Patricia Langford; or
>
> \(c\) Directly to any member of the Compliance Committee.

**Non-Retaliation Policy.** Greenfield strictly prohibits retaliation against any individual who, in good faith, reports a compliance concern, participates in a compliance investigation, or refuses to participate in conduct that the individual believes violates applicable law or this Manual. Any Practice Personnel who engages in retaliation against a reporter shall be subject to disciplinary action, up to and including termination.

**[6.3 Investigation Procedures]{.underline}**

All compliance reports received through the hotline or other reporting channels shall be handled in accordance with the following investigation procedures:

**Step 1: Logging.** Upon receipt of a compliance report, the CCO shall log the report in the compliance hotline tracking system. The log entry shall include the date of the report, the reporting channel (hotline

, email, direct communication), whether the report was anonymous or identified, and a summary of the reported concern.

**Step 2: Preliminary Assessment.** The CCO shall conduct a preliminary assessment to determine the nature and severity of the reported concern. The preliminary assessment shall evaluate whether the reported conduct, if substantiated, would constitute a potential violation of the Stark Law, Anti-Kickback Statute, False Claims Act, or other applicable law.

**Step 3: Notification to the Compliance Committee.** For reports involving potential violations of the Stark Law, Anti-Kickback Statute, or False Claims Act, the CCO shall promptly notify the Compliance Committee and, where appropriate, consult with outside legal counsel. Notification to the Committee shall occur within five (5) business days of receipt of the report.

**Step 4: Investigation.** Where the preliminary assessment indicates that a full investigation is warranted, the CCO shall conduct or coordinate a thorough investigation, which may include: (a) interviews with relevant personnel; (b) review of relevant documents, records, and data; (c) consultation with outside legal counsel or subject matter experts; and (d) any other investigative steps appropriate to the circumstances.

**Step 5: Documentation.** All investigations shall be documented, including a written summary of the factual findings, legal analysis (where applicable), conclusions, and any recommended corrective actions. Investigation documentation shall be maintained in the compliance records in accordance with the retention policy set forth in Section 6.4.

**Step 6: Committee Review.** The Compliance Committee shall review the findings and recommendations of all investigations involving potential violations of federal or state healthcare law and shall determine appropriate corrective action. The Committee\'s review and determination shall be documented in the Committee meeting minutes.

**Step 7: Corrective Action.** Where an investigation identifies a compliance deficiency, corrective action shall be implemented in accordance with Section 9 of this Manual.

**Step 8: Resolution and Closure.** Upon completion of the investigation and implementation of any necessary corrective action, the CCO shall close the matter in the compliance hotline tracking system and document the resolution.

**Timeline.** Investigations shall be completed within sixty (60) days of receipt of the initial report, unless extended by the Compliance Committee for good cause. Extensions shall be documented and the reasons for the extension recorded.

**Quarterly Reporting.** The CCO shall present a summary of all hotline reports and investigation outcomes at each quarterly Compliance Committee meeting. The summary shall include the number of reports received, the nature of the reported concerns, the status of pending investigations, and the outcomes of completed investigations.

**[6.4 Record Retention]{.underline}**

All compliance reports, investigation files, and corrective action documentation shall be retained for a minimum of seven (7) years from the date of resolution. Records shall be maintained in a secure, confidential database accessible only to the CCO and Compliance Committee members. Access to compliance records shall be restricted to protect the confidentiality of reporters and the integrity of investigations.

**[Section 7: Compliance Training and Education]{.underline}**

**[7.1 Annual Training Requirement]{.underline}**

All Greenfield physicians, staff, and contractors are required to complete annual compliance training. The annual training program shall cover, at a minimum, the following topics:

> \(a\) Overview of the Stark Law, Anti-Kickback Statute, and False Claims Act, including recent developments and enforcement trends;
>
> \(b\) Greenfield-specific compliance policies and procedures, including the provisions of this Compliance Program Manual;
>
> \(c\) Reporting obligations and use of the compliance hotline;
>
> \(d\) The non-retaliation policy;
>
> \(e\) In-office ancillary services requirements, including supervision and billing;
>
> \(f\) Fair market value and commercial reasonableness requirements for compensation and lease arrangements;
>
> \(g\) Consequences of non-compliance, including civil monetary penalties, exclusion, and potential criminal liability; and
>
> \(h\) Any other compliance topics identified by the CCO or the Compliance Committee as relevant to the Practice\'s operations and risk profile.

Annual compliance training shall be conducted no later than the end of the first quarter of each calendar year. Attendance at annual compliance training is mandatory for all Practice Personnel. The CCO shall maintain records of training completion, including the date of training, the topics covered, the names and titles of attendees, and copies of training materials.

Practice Personnel who fail to complete required compliance training within the prescribed timeframe may be subject to disciplinary action. The CCO shall report training completion rates to the Compliance Committee at the first quarterly meeting following the training deadline.

**[7.2 New Hire Orientation]{.underline}**

All new physicians, staff, and contractors shall receive compliance orientation within thirty (30) days of their start date. The orientation shall cover the contents of this Compliance Program Manual, the compliance hotline and reporting channels, the non-retaliation policy, and the new hire\'s obligations under the Compliance Program. Each new hire shall sign the Acknowledgment Form attached as Appendix C, confirming receipt and understanding of this Manual.

**[7.3 Specialized Training]{.underline}**

Physicians and staff involved in specific areas of heightened compliance risk shall receive specialized training on applicable legal requirements beyond the annual general compliance training. Areas of specialized training may include:

> • **Billing and Coding Personnel:** Detailed training on proper coding practices, claim submission requirements, and the identification of potential billing errors or irregularities.
>
> • **Lease Administration Personnel:** Training on Stark Law rental exceptions and FMV documentation requirements.
>
> • **Compensation Committee Members:** Training on FMV benchmarking, the volume-or-value prohibition, and permissible physician compensation structures.
>
> • **Site Managers:** Training on supervision requirements for in-office ancillary services.

The CCO shall identify specialized training needs as part of the annual compliance risk assessment and shall coordinate the delivery of specialized training as appropriate.

**[Section 8: Compliance Auditing and Risk Assessment]{.underline}**

**[8.1 Annual Compliance Risk Assessment]{.underline}**

The CCO shall conduct a comprehensive compliance risk assessment at least annually. The purpose of the risk assessment is to identify areas of heightened compliance risk across all aspects of the Practice\'s operations and to prioritize compliance activities and resources accordingly.

The annual risk assessment shall address, at a minimum, the following areas:

> \(a\) **Physician Compensation Arrangements.** Assessment of all physician compensation arrangements for compliance with FMV requirements and the prohibition on compensation tied to the volume or value of referrals.
>
> \(b\) **Lease and Space-Sharing Arrangements.** Assessment of all lease agreements with entities to or from which Greenfield physicians make referrals, including leases with ClearView Diagnostic Imaging, LLC, Pinnacle Reference Laboratory, Inc., and Ohio Heart & Vascular Associates, for compliance with the rental of office space exception and FMV requirements.
>
> \(c\) **In-Office Ancillary Services.** Assessment of supervision compliance, billing practices, and group practice membership requirements at all locations furnishing DHS.
>
> \(d\) **Affiliated Entity Relationships.** Assessment of the Practice\'s relationship with Buckeye Surgical Center, LLC, including physician ownership interests and referral patterns.
>
> \(e\) **Referral Patterns.** Assessment of referral patterns between Greenfield physicians and entities with which the Practice has financial relationships, to identify any patterns that may suggest improper inducement or non-compliance.
>
> \(f\) **Billing and Coding Practices.** Assessment of billing accuracy, coding compliance, and claims submission practices.

The compliance risk assessment shall be completed no later than the end of the second quarter of each calendar year and presented to the Compliance Committee at its next regularly scheduled meeting. The risk assessment report shall identify specific areas of concern, assign risk levels, and recommend targeted compliance activities, audits, or corrective actions.

**[8.2 Internal Compliance Audits]{.underline}**

In addition to the annual risk assessment, the CCO shall coordinate periodic internal compliance audits of specific arrangements or practice areas identified as high risk. Internal audits may include, without limitation:

> • Review of physician compensation arrangements against current FMV benchmarks and applicable MGMA or other survey data;
>
> • Review of lease agreements against current FMV appraisals to verify that rental rates remain within FMV and are not correlated to referral volume;
>
> • Review of in-office ancillary services supervision logs and site visit findings to verify compliance with supervision requirements;
>
> • Review of referral data to identify patterns or anomalies in referral relationships between Greenfield and affiliated entities or tenants;
>
> • Review of billing data to verify that DHS is billed under the group NPI and in compliance with applicable coding and documentation requirements.

Audit findings shall be documented in a written report and presented to the Compliance Committee. For any identified deficiencies, the CCO shall develop a corrective action plan, including specific remediation steps, responsible parties, and timelines for completion. The Compliance Committee shall review and approve corrective action plans and monitor their implementation.

The last full internal compliance audit was conducted in March 2022. Subsequent audits shall be conducted as determined by the CCO and Compliance Committee based on the results of the annual risk assessment.

**[8.3 External Audits]{.underline}**

Greenfield may engage external auditors or independent consultants to perform compliance audits where the Compliance Committee determines that external expertise is warranted. Redstone Accounting Group, LLP serves as Greenfield\'s external auditor for annual financial audits and may be engaged for compliance-related financial analyses. The Compliance Committee may also engage specialized healthcare compliance consultants, law firms, or valuation firms for targeted reviews of specific arrangements or practice areas.

The engagement of external auditors shall be coordinated by the CCO with the approval of the Compliance Committee. External audit reports shall be presented to the Compliance Committee and treated as confidential compliance records.

**[Section 9: Corrective Action and Disciplinary Procedures]{.underline}**

**[9.1 Corrective Action]{.underline}**

When compliance deficiencies are identified through internal audits, risk assessments, investigations, hotline reports, or any other means, the CCO and Compliance Committee shall implement appropriate corrective action. Corrective actions may include, without limitation:

> \(a\) Amendment or restructuring of non-compliant financial arrangements, including compensation agreements and lease agreements, to bring them into compliance with applicable Stark Law exceptions and AKS safe harbors;
>
> \(b\) Termination of non-compliant arrangements where amendment is insufficient to achieve compliance;
>
> \(c\) Revision of Practice policies and procedures to address identified gaps;
>
> \(d\) Additional or targeted training for affected personnel;
>
> \(e\) Disciplinary action against individuals responsible for or contributing to the non-compliance, as described in Section 9.2;
>
> \(f\) Voluntary self-disclosure to applicable government agencies, including CMS, the Office of Inspector General, and/or the Department of Justice, where appropriate and as determined by the Compliance Committee in consultation with outside legal counsel;
>
> \(g\) Repayment of overpayments or amounts improperly received as a result of the non-compliant arrangement;
>
> \(h\) Enhanced monitoring and auditing of the affected area to prevent recurrence.

Corrective action plans shall be documented in writing, shall include specific remediation steps, assigned responsible parties, and timelines for completion, and shall be approved by the Compliance Committee. The CCO shall monitor the implementation of corrective action plans and report on progress to the Compliance Committee at each quarterly meeting.

**[9.2 Disciplinary Policy]{.underline}**

Violations of this Compliance Program Manual, applicable healthcare laws, or the Practice\'s policies and procedures may result in disciplinary action. Disciplinary measures shall be proportionate to the nature and severity of the violation and shall be applied consistently across all Practice Personnel regardless of position, title, or tenure.

Disciplinary actions may include, without limitation:

> • Verbal or written warning
>
> • Mandatory additional compliance training
>
> • Suspension with or without pay
>
> • Reduction in compensation or bonus
>
> • Termination of employment
>
> • Expulsion from membership in the Practice (for member/owner physicians, subject to the terms of the Operating Agreement)
>
> • Referral to appropriate professional licensing authorities

All disciplinary actions shall be documented in the affected individual\'s personnel file and in the compliance records. The Compliance Committee shall be notified of all disciplinary actions taken in connection with compliance violations.

**[Section 10: Government Investigations and Voluntary Disclosure]{.underline}**

**[10.1 Responding to Government Inquiries]{.underline}**

In the event that any Practice Personnel receives a government inquiry, subpoena, civil investigative demand, search warrant, or other indication of a government investigation relating to the Practice\'s operations, the following procedures shall be followed:

> \(a\) **Immediate Notification.** The individual receiving or becoming aware of the government contact shall immediately notify the Chief Compliance Officer and the Chair of the Compliance Committee. Notification shall occur on the same business day as the receipt of the government contact, or as soon as practicable thereafter.
>
> \(b\) **Preservation of Documents.** Upon notification of a government inquiry, all Practice Personnel shall preserve all documents, records, electronic files, and communications that may be relevant to the inquiry. No documents shall be destroyed, altered, concealed, or removed from Practice premises. The CCO shall issue a formal document preservation notice to all affected personnel.
>
> \(c\) **Coordination Through Counsel.** All communications with government agents, investigators, or attorneys shall be coordinated through outside legal counsel engaged by the Practice. No Practice Personnel shall provide substantive responses to government inquiries, participate in interviews, or produce documents without the prior involvement and guidance of outside counsel.
>
> \(d\) **Cooperation.** Subject to the advice of outside counsel, the Practice shall cooperate with lawful government inquiries and investigations in a manner consistent with the Practice\'s legal rights and obligations.

**[10.2 Voluntary Self-Disclosure]{.underline}**

Greenfield is committed to transparency and, where appropriate, will consider voluntary self-disclosure of identified compliance issues to the applicable government agency. Decisions regarding voluntary self-disclosure shall be made by the Compliance Committee in consultation with outside legal counsel, taking into account the nature and scope of the identified issue, the potential legal and financial implications, and the interests of the Practice and its patients.

The Practice recognizes that voluntary self-disclosure may mitigate potential liability and demonstrates good faith commitment to compliance. The Compliance Committee shall evaluate self-disclosure options on a case-by-case basis.

**[Section 11: Record Keeping and Documentation]{.underline}**

**[11.1 Compliance Documentation]{.underline}**

The CCO shall maintain comprehensive records of all compliance activities undertaken pursuant to this Manual. Compliance documentation shall include, without limitation:

> • Compliance Committee meeting agendas and minutes
>
> • Compliance training records, including attendance rosters, training materials, and completion certifications
>
> • Compliance hotline reports, investigation files, and resolution documentation
>
> • Internal and external audit reports and risk assessments
>
> • Corrective action plans and implementation records
>
> • Fair market value appraisals, benchmarking studies, and compensation analyses
>
> • Written agreements for all financial relationships subject to the Stark Law and Anti-Kickback Statute, including physician employment agreements, independent contractor agreements, medical directorship agreements, and lease agreements
>
> • Supervision logs from Practice locations furnishing DHS
>
> • Correspondence with government agencies, outside counsel, and external consultants relating to compliance matters

All compliance documentation shall be organized and maintained in a centralized compliance file system, whether electronic or physical, under the control of the CCO. Access to compliance documentation shall be limited to the CCO, members of the Compliance Committee, and outside legal counsel as needed.

**[11.2 Retention Period]{.underline}**

All compliance records shall be retained for a minimum of seven (7) years from the date of creation or the date of termination or expiration of the relevant arrangement, whichever is later. This retention period applies to all categories of compliance documentation described in Section 11.1.

Upon expiration of the applicable retention period, records may be destroyed in accordance with the Practice\'s general document retention and destruction policies. No compliance records shall be destroyed while any government investigation, audit, or legal proceeding relating to the subject matter of the records is pending or reasonably anticipated.

**[Section 12: Amendments and Updates]{.underline}**

This Compliance Program Manual may be amended from time to time by action of the Compliance Committee. Any amendments to this Manual shall be approved by the Compliance Committee and communicated to all Practice Personnel. Amendments shall be effective upon the date of approval by the Committee, unless a different effective date is specified.

This Manual shall be reviewed annually by the Compliance Committee and updated as necessary to reflect changes in applicable law, regulation, guidance, or Practice operations. The annual review shall be completed no later than the end of the first quarter of each calendar year, and any resulting updates shall be distributed to all Practice Personnel promptly following approval.

All Practice Personnel shall be notified of amendments to this Manual and shall be required to acknowledge receipt and understanding of any material changes. The CCO shall maintain a record of all amendments, including the date of each amendment, the sections affected, and a summary of the changes made.

**[Appendix A: Key Definitions]{.underline}**

The following definitions apply throughout this Compliance Program Manual:

**Anti-Kickback Statute (AKS).** The federal statute codified at 42 U.S.C. § 1320a-7b(b), which prohibits the knowing and willful offer, payment, solicitation, or receipt of remuneration to induce or reward referrals for items or services reimbursable under federal healthcare programs.

**Compensation Arrangement.** Any arrangement involving any remuneration between a physician (or an immediate family member of a physician) and an entity. Remuneration includes any payment or other benefit made directly or indirectly, overtly or covertly, in cash or in kind. A compensation arrangement may be direct or indirect.

**Designated Health Services (DHS).** The following categories of services, as defined by 42 U.S.C. § 1395nn(h)(6) and the implementing regulations: (1) clinical laboratory services; (2) physical therapy services; (3) occupational therapy services; (4) outpatient speech-language pathology services; (5) radiology and certain other imaging services; (6) radiation therapy services and supplies; (7) durable medical equipment and supplies; (8) parenteral and enteral nutrients, equipment, and supplies; (9) prosthetics, orthotics, and prosthetic devices and supplies; (10) home health services; (11) outpatient prescription drugs; and (12) inpatient and outpatient hospital services.

**Fair Market Value (FMV).** The value in arm\'s-length transactions, consistent with the general market value. \"General market value\" means: (a) with respect to compensation for services, the compensation that would be included in a service agreement as the result of bona fide bargaining between well-informed parties to the agreement who are not otherwise in a position to generate business for the other party; and (b) with respect to the rental of equipment or office space, the rental price that rental equipment or office space would bring as the result of bona fide bargaining between well-informed parties who are not otherwise in a position to generate business for the other party.

**False Claims Act (FCA).** The federal statute codified at 31 U.S.C. §§ 3729--3733, which imposes civil liability on persons and entities that knowingly submit or cause the submission of false or fraudulent claims for payment to the United States government.

**Financial Relationship.** As defined by the Stark Law, either (a) an ownership or investment interest in an entity, or (b) a compensation arrangement between a physician (or immediate family member) and an entity.

**Group Practice.** As defined in 42 C.F.R. § 411.352, a group of two or more physicians legally organized as a partnership, professional corporation, foundation, not-for-profit corporation, faculty practice plan, or similar association, that meets the requirements of the regulation, including the \"substantially all\" test and unified business requirements.

**Immediate Family Member.** As defined in the Stark Law regulations at 42 C.F.R. § 411.351, a husband or wife; birth or adoptive parent, child, or sibling; stepparent, stepchild, stepbrother, or stepsister; father-in-law, mother-in-law, son-in-law, daughter-in-law, brother-in-law, or sister-in-law; grandparent or grandchild; and spouse of a grandparent or grandchild.

**Referral.** As defined by the Stark Law, the request by a physician for, or ordering of, or the certifying or recertifying of the need for, any designated health service, including the request by a physician for a consultation with another physician and any test or procedure ordered by or to be performed by (or under the supervision of) that other physician. A referral also includes a request or establishment of a plan of care by a physician that includes the provision of DHS.

**Remuneration.** Anything of value in any form whatsoever, whether made directly or indirectly, overtly or covertly, in cash or in kind, including but not limited to transfers of items or services for free or for other than fair market value.

**Stark Law.** The federal physician self-referral statute codified at 42 U.S.C. § 1395nn and its implementing regulations at 42 C.F.R. Part 411, Subparts B and J.

**Volume or Value of Referrals.** The standard under the Stark Law that compensation must not be determined in a manner that takes into account the volume or value of referrals by the physician to the entity, or other business generated between the parties. Compensation that varies with or is correlated to the number of referrals or the revenue generated from referred services violates this standard, unless a specific regulatory exception permits such correlation (e.g., productivity bonuses for personally performed services under the employment exception).

**[Appendix B: Compliance Hotline Contact Information]{.underline}**

**Telephone:** 1-888-555-0147

The compliance hotline is available Monday through Friday, 8:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m. Eastern Time. Voicemail messages may be left outside of normal business hours and will be retrieved and logged by the CCO on the next business day.

**Email:** compliance@greenfieldhealth.com

Email reports are monitored by the CCO during normal business hours. Email reports received outside of business hours will be reviewed on the next business day.

**Written Reports:** Written compliance reports may be submitted by mail to:

> Patricia Langford Chief Compliance Officer Greenfield Health Partners, LLC 2800 Riverside Medical Plaza, Suite 400 Columbus, OH 43215

Written reports should be marked \"CONFIDENTIAL --- COMPLIANCE REPORT\" on the envelope.

**Response Time.** The CCO shall acknowledge receipt of all compliance reports (other than anonymous reports for which no contact information is provided) within three (3) business days. All reports shall be logged in the compliance tracking system within one (1) business day of receipt.

**Non-Retaliation.** Greenfield Health Partners, LLC strictly prohibits retaliation against any individual who, in good faith, reports a suspected compliance violation through the hotline or any other reporting channel. Individuals who believe they have been subjected to retaliation should report the retaliation through the compliance hotline or directly to any member of the Compliance Committee.

**[Appendix C: Acknowledgment Form]{.underline}**

**GREENFIELD HEALTH PARTNERS, LLC** **COMPLIANCE PROGRAM MANUAL --- ACKNOWLEDGMENT FORM**

I, the undersigned, hereby acknowledge that I have received a copy of the Greenfield Health Partners, LLC Compliance Program Manual (adopted April 15, 2021). I have read and understand the contents of the Manual, including my obligations to comply with all applicable federal and state healthcare laws, the Practice\'s compliance policies and procedures, and the reporting requirements described in the Manual.

I understand that I am required to report any suspected compliance violations through the compliance hotline or other reporting channels described in the Manual, and that Greenfield prohibits retaliation against individuals who report compliance concerns in good faith.

I agree to comply with the provisions of the Compliance Program Manual in the performance of my duties on behalf of Greenfield Health Partners, LLC.
