P('**Record-currency caveat.** The documents we reviewed run through about October 2024. The latest are the Hale complaint (filed Oct. 18, 2024) and the CCO’s October 2024 confirmation, noted in Exhibit B to the Greenfield Operating Agreement, that no Compensation Committee charter exists. Several arrangements discussed below have since expired by their own terms: the Pinnacle lease on Feb. 28, 2025, the ClearView lease on Dec. 31, 2025, and the Wellford employment agreement on Jan. 14, 2024. Some may be in holdover or may have been renewed or restructured. We have no documents after October 2024 and no information on the status of the qui tam (seal, intervention decision or service). Where this memorandum refers to the “current” state of an arrangement, it means as of the last document in the file.')

H('I. Questions Presented and Short Answers', 1)
P('**1. Do Greenfield’s physician compensation, ownership, lease and in-kind arrangements comply with the Stark Law, 42 U.S.C. § 1395nn, and 42 C.F.R. Part 411, Subpart J?** No. Several do not, and one defect reaches the whole practice. The “Referral Quality Bonus” (RQB) pays employed physicians $150 per completed internal referral, including referrals to Greenfield’s own laboratory and imaging services. That is a per-referral payment that takes into account the volume of designated health services (DHS) referrals. It is fatal to the employment exception for every employed physician who receives it (42 C.F.R. § 411.357(c)). More important, it very likely disqualifies Greenfield as a “group practice” under 42 C.F.R. § 411.352(g). If Greenfield is not a group practice, the in-office ancillary services exception (IOASE, § 411.355(b)) is unavailable to all 87 physicians, members and employees alike, for every Medicare DHS referral to Greenfield’s in-house laboratory and imaging services from January 1, 2022 forward. Other material issues:')
B('the Pinnacle Reference Laboratory lease, which is below fair market value (FMV) and rests on a stale appraisal that the lease misdescribes;')
B('an undocumented free courier service that Pinnacle provides to all 12 Greenfield locations;')
B('referral-based profit distributions at Buckeye Surgical Center and the “Referral Credit” allocation inside Greenfield (mainly AKS, with some Stark spillover);')
B('an unbenchmarked $120,000-per-year medical directorship held by the Managing Member, about $1,250 per contracted hour;')
B('IOASE location and supervision gaps at the Hilliard and Dublin satellites;')
B('the billing and IOASE posture of four independent-contractor radiologists;')
B('a compliance program that has largely stopped operating.')
P('**2. What is the likely exposure?** Stark is a strict-liability statute. Medicare may not pay for DHS furnished on a prohibited referral, and amounts collected must be refunded (42 U.S.C. § 1395nn(g)(1)–(2)). Civil monetary penalties apply per service and per circumvention scheme (§ 1395nn(g)(3)–(4)). If the claims were knowingly submitted, the FCA adds treble damages and per-claim penalties. The relator alleges more than $30 million in tainted Medicare claims for 2023 alone (Compl. ¶ 107). Several of the relator’s theories are overstated or legally flawed (Part V). But the group-practice consequence of the RQB, which the relator has not yet pleaded clearly, could support an even larger refund base than she alleges. That base is all Greenfield DHS from January 2022, not just DHS traceable to referrals by RQB recipients. Exposure cannot be quantified from the file. Medicare DHS revenue by service line and year is the critical missing data point.')
P('**3. What should Greenfield do?** Act immediately, under privilege and through outside counsel:')
B('suspend the RQB and the Buckeye Referral Credit;')
B('impose a litigation hold;')
B('protect the relator against any appearance of retaliation;')
B('remove conflicted fiduciaries from compliance oversight;')
B('commission an independent, privileged look-back (claims, FMV and data reconciliation);')
B('restructure each defective arrangement on a documented FMV basis;')
B('make a disclosure decision promptly, under the 60-day overpayment rule and in light of the pending qui tam. Disclosure options include the CMS Self-Referral Disclosure Protocol (SRDP), the OIG Self-Disclosure Protocol (SDP), and direct engagement with the U.S. Attorney’s Office for credit under the DOJ’s FCA cooperation policy.')
P('A prioritized remediation plan appears in Part VII.')

 ['5', 'Buckeye ASC: distributions by “Referral Percentage”; Greenfield “Referral Credit” of 0.5% of facility fees per referred case', 'AKS / ASC safe harbor § 1001.952(r); § 411.352(g)/(i) spillover; FCA', 'Critical (AKS) / Medium (Stark)', 'Buckeye OA §§ 1.9, 1.25–1.26, 4.1–4.5, 6.2; Greenfield OA § 8.4; Comp. Summary', 'Suspend credit; amend both operating agreements to pro rata ownership; consider OIG SDP'],
 ['6', 'Stein Medical Director Agreement: $120,000/yr for 96 hrs (= $1,250/hr) since 2016, never re-benchmarked; conflicted approvals', 'AKS § 1001.952(d); possible indirect compensation under § 411.354(c)(2)', 'High', 'MDA §§ 2.2–2.3, 3.2, 4.1, Ex. A; Buckeye OA § 5.4; Greenfield OA § 10.1', 'Independent FMV review; collect time logs; recusal; amend'],
 ['7', 'Hilliard and Dublin satellites: daily lab testing; physician on site ~2 days/wk (Hilliard) and ~3 half-days/wk (Dublin)', '§ 411.355(b)(1)–(2) (furnishing, supervision, “same building”); CLIA; Manual § 5.2', 'High', 'Audit memo § III.A (Mar. 2022), not remediated', 'Restrict testing; quantify; CLIA and building-test review'],
 ['8', 'Four 1099 radiologists (~60% of their time at Greenfield; ~30% of imaging reads) billed under the group NPI', '§ 411.351 / § 411.355(b); anti-markup rule § 414.50; reassignment § 424.80', 'Medium', 'Audit memo § III.B; Hotline #2023-11; Comp.  ['9', 'ClearView lease: $18/sf triple-net vs. FSG appraisal; FMV likely defensible but undocumented', '§ 411.357(a); AKS', 'Medium', 'ClearView Lease §§ 4.1–4.6, 5.1–5.3, 7.1, Ex.  ['10', 'Member compensation governance: self-approval; quality bonuses above the 25% cap for both physician Compensation Committee members; 2019 benchmarks', 'AKS; § 411.352(i) documentation; fiduciary', 'Medium', 'OA §§ 7.2–7.3; Comp. Summary rows 1–2', 'Independent comp review; recusal; true-up'],
 ['11', 'Compliance program breakdown: Stark hotline reports closed without Committee or counsel review; no training or risk assessments; meetings skipped', 'OIG GCPG (2023); FCA scienter; Manual §§ 2, 6–8', 'High', 'Hotline log 2023; email chain Sept. 2024; audit memo', 'Reconstitute oversight; reopen hotline matters under counsel'],
 ['12', 'Records and data integrity (ownership tables, counts, totals)', 'Evidence and credibility; § 411.352(i)(4) documentation', 'Medium', 'Comp. Summary; Buckeye OA Ex. A; OA § 3.1', 'Forensic reconciliation under privilege'],
], widths=[0.25, 1.45, 1.2, 0.65, 1.55, 1.4], fs=7.5)

H('III. Background and Documents Reviewed', 1)
H('A. The organization', 2)
P('Greenfield Health Partners, LLC is an Ohio LLC formed March 14, 2009. Its Amended and Restated Operating Agreement is effective January 1, 2020 (“OA”). It is a multispecialty group: orthopedics, cardiology, internal medicine, radiology, general surgery, urology and neurology. It has 12 Columbus-area locations and reports 87 physicians. The governing documents count 52 members and 35 employed physicians. The 2023 compensation summary lists 52 members, 31 employed physicians and 4 independent-contractor (IC) radiologists. Greenfield bills all services under a single group NPI and TIN. It operates in-office clinical laboratory and point-of-care testing at 8 of 12 sites and diagnostic imaging (OA § 10.2; audit memo § III). It relies on the IOASE for those DHS. Greenfield also owns and is landlord of the 48,000 sf Riverside Medical Plaza. It leases space there to ClearView Diagnostic Imaging (Suite 210), Pinnacle Reference Laboratory (Suite 105) and Ohio Heart & Vascular Associates (Suite 310).')
P('Greenfield owns 60% of Buckeye Surgical Center, LLC (the ASC), formed August 22, 2016, and serves as its Manager. Dr. Raymond K. Stein owns 25% personally and Dr. Priya Narayan owns 15% (Buckeye OA § 3.1). Dr. Stein is Greenfield’s Managing Member and CMO (4.2% interest), Buckeye’s Medical Director, chair of Greenfield’s Compensation Committee, and chair of its Compliance Committee. Dr. Narayan (3.1% interest) sits on both committees. The CFO, identified in the documents as “Alan Cromdale Consulting”, sits on both committees and negotiated the ClearView and Pinnacle leases. The CFO’s e-mail address is amercer@greenfieldhealth.com. Whether the CFO is an individual employee or an outsourced consulting firm should be confirmed, because it bears on governance, privilege and witness planning. Patricia Langford has been CCO since April 2021.')
H('B. Documents reviewed', 2)
T(['Document', 'Date', 'Relevance'], [

 ['Amended & Restated Operating Agreement of Buckeye Surgical Center (excerpts)', 'Eff. Aug. 22, 2016 (never amended)', 'Referral-Percentage allocations and distributions; Greenfield internal referral-credit representation; Medical Director'],

 ['Physician Compensation Summary 2023 (CFO office)', 'Prepared Feb. 15, 2024', 'Physician-level 2023 compensation, RQB, Referral Credits, ownership'],

/home/user/Lawless_Research_Lab/harvey_lab/sbx.sh /home/user/Lawless_Research_Lab/harvey_lab/vendor/harvey-labs/results/healthcare-life-sciences/identify-stark-law-compliance-issues/claude-code-session/20261015-115344 "cat > /workspace/part2.py <<'EOF'
H('IV. Governing Legal Framework (Summary)', 1)
P('**Stark Law.** Absent an applicable exception, a physician may not refer a Medicare patient for DHS to an entity with which the physician (or an immediate family member) has a financial relationship. The entity may not bill Medicare for DHS furnished on a prohibited referral (42 U.S.C. § 1395nn(a)(1); 42 C.F.R. § 411.353). Clinical laboratory and radiology/imaging services are DHS. Services paid as part of the ASC composite rate are excluded from DHS (42 C.F.R. § 411.351, definition of “designated health services”). A “referral” includes a request for a consultation with another physician and any test or procedure ordered by that consultant (§ 411.351). The statute imposes strict liability. The sanctions are:')
B('denial of payment and an obligation to refund (§ 1395nn(g)(1)–(2));')
B('civil monetary penalties per service billed with knowledge, and per circumvention scheme (§ 1395nn(g)(3)–(4)), as inflation-adjusted under 45 C.F.R. Part 102;')
B('exclusion.')
P('The Medicaid analogue is 42 U.S.C. § 1396b(s). Since the CMS final rule effective January 19, 2021, compensation “takes into account” the volume or value of referrals only if the formula uses referrals as a variable and the compensation rises or falls with them (§ 411.354(d)(5)–(6)). A per-referral payment is the paradigm case.')
P('**Group practice and IOASE.** The IOASE (§ 411.355(b)) protects both ownership and compensation relationships for in-office DHS. It is available only if Greenfield qualifies as a “group practice” under § 411.352. Among other requirements:')
B('the members of the group, taken in the aggregate, must furnish at least 75% of their total patient care services through the group (§ 411.352(d));')
B('no physician who is a member of the group may receive compensation directly or indirectly based on the volume or value of his or her DHS referrals, except through a profit share or productivity bonus that meets § 411.352(i) (§ 411.352(g)).')
P('“Members of the group” are owners and employees. Independent contractors are not members; they may be “physicians in the group practice” (§ 411.351). The IOASE also requires that the DHS be:')
B('furnished personally by the referring physician or a group member, or by individuals supervised in accordance with applicable Medicare payment and coverage rules (§ 411.355(b)(1));')
B('furnished in the “same building” under one of three alternative tests, or in a “centralized building” (§ 411.355(b)(2));')
B('billed by the group under its billing number (§ 411.355(b)(3)).')
P('**Other relevant Stark exceptions.**')
B('Bona fide employment, § 411.357(c): identifiable services; FMV; not determined in any manner that takes into account the volume or value of referrals; commercially reasonable. There is no writing or “set in advance” element, but the directed-referral rules in § 411.354(d)(4) require a writing if compensation is conditioned on referrals to a particular provider.')
B('Rental of office space, § 411.357(a): signed writing, term of at least one year, exclusive use, rental charges set in advance and consistent with FMV, not tied to referrals, commercially reasonable, holdover protection.')
B('Personal service arrangements and FMV compensation, § 411.357(d) and (l).')
P('Physician owners of a “physician organization” (Greenfield) “stand in the shoes” of that organization. A Greenfield lease with a DHS entity is therefore analyzed as a direct compensation arrangement between each Greenfield owner and that DHS entity (§ 411.354(c)).')
P('**AKS and FCA.** The AKS, 42 U.S.C. § 1320a-7b(b), is an intent-based felony statute. In most circuits it is violated if *one purpose* of the remuneration is to induce referrals. Safe harbors appear at 42 C.F.R. § 1001.952, including (b) space rental, (d) personal services, (i) employees and (r) ASCs. Claims “resulting from” an AKS violation are false under the FCA (42 U.S.C. § 1320a-7b(g)). Circuits are split on the causation standard for AKS-tainted claims, and the current Sixth Circuit position should be confirmed. Stark-tainted claims are false without any intent showing for the underlying violation, but FCA liability requires that the claims be submitted “knowingly” (31 U.S.C. § 3729(b)(1)). Under 42 U.S.C. § 1320a-7k(d) and 42 C.F.R. § 401.305, an identified overpayment must be reported and returned within 60 days of identification, subject to the six-year lookback. The rule as amended effective January 1, 2025 allows up to 180 days of suspension for a timely, good-faith investigation. An overpayment that is retained becomes an FCA “reverse false claim” (31 U.S.C. § 3729(a)(1)(G)).')

H('V. Analysis of Issues', 1)

# ---------------- ISSUE 1
H('Issue 1 — The “Referral Quality Bonus” Is a Per-Referral Payment That Defeats the Employment Exception (Critical)', 2)
H('Facts', 3)
B('The Compensation Plan Update Memorandum is dated January 10, 2022 and is signed by Dr. Stein and the CFO. It says the plan was approved by the Compensation Committee on December 14, 2021 and is effective January 1, 2022, i.e., retroactively. It pays every employed (non-member) physician **$150 per “Qualified Internal Referral”**, calculated and paid quarterly, capped at **$90,000 per physician per year (600 referrals)** (§§ 4.1–4.4).')
B('A “Qualified Internal Referral” is a referral to (a) a Greenfield member or employed specialist, (b) Buckeye Surgical Center, or (c) **Greenfield’s in-office ancillary services: clinical laboratory, point-of-care testing and diagnostic imaging** (§ 4.2). The referral counts only if the service is **completed and billed** (§§ 4.2, 5(c)). The billing department tracks referrals by category: specialist, Buckeye, ancillary (§ 5).')
B('There is no quality component. Payment is triggered by the referral order, the patient’s appearance and the billing of the service. Nothing in the memo measures clinical appropriateness, outcomes or guideline adherence. The memo’s own rationale is to “compensat[e] physicians for each Qualified Internal Referral” (§ 4.5).')
B('The memo states that “[n]o amendment to your individual employment agreement is required” (§ 7). The Wellford agreement, signed five days after the memo, does not mention the RQB:')
B('§ 4.3 permits added compensation only by written amendment or by a plan “consistent with … 42 U.S.C. § 1395nn”;', 1)
B('§ 4.6 prohibits any remuneration “in connection with … Physician’s referral of patients for designated health services”;', 1)
B('Exhibit B describes base salary, productivity bonus and benefits as “all compensation payable.”', 1)
B('OA § 7.5(c) authorizes the RQB “to reward Employed Physicians who maintain robust referral networks.” The OA is stated to be effective January 1, 2020, two years before the December 2021 approval, and also defines “Qualified Internal Referral.” Either the OA was changed without the two-thirds written amendment that OA § 14.1 requires, or a referral-based bonus was contemplated (and possibly paid) before 2022. Either way, the look-back may need to start before 2022.')
B('**2023 payments:** $1,260,000 to 31 employed physicians, equal to **8,400 paid referrals**. Of that, $712,500 (57%) went to 12 internal-medicine physicians. Examples:')
B('Dr. Martinez was paid at the $90,000 cap;', 1)
B('Dr. Wellford received $78,000 (520 referrals). That is 27% of his $285,000 base and almost double his $42,000 productivity bonus.', 1)
B('The March 31, 2022 internal audit reviewed the RQB and found “[n]o compliance concerns” (§ V). Hotline report #2023-07 (Apr. 12, 2023) called the RQB “a kickback for referrals.” The CCO closed it in 16 days as “a legitimate quality metric,” with no Compliance Committee review and no counsel. That violated Manual § 6.3, Steps 3 and 6 (Committee notice within five business days for Stark/AKS reports; Committee review of findings).')
H('Analysis', 3)
P('**Employment exception fails.** Compensation that pays a fixed dollar amount for each referral uses referrals as a variable and rises with them. Under § 411.354(d)(5)(i) it “takes into account the volume or value of referrals” per se. The RQB counts DHS referrals in two ways:')
B('directly, through referrals to Greenfield’s in-house laboratory and imaging;')
B('indirectly, through referrals to Greenfield specialists. Under § 411.351, any test the consulting specialist orders is itself a referral by the requesting physician.')
P('No employed physician receiving the RQB can satisfy § 411.357(c)(4) (the volume/value standard), and the productivity carve-out applies only to personally performed services. The RQB is also not FMV for any identifiable service. It pays for the referral, not for work, and the only benchmarking study (Lakeshore, November 2019) predates the program and did not evaluate it (Compl. ¶ 39; Comp. Memo § 1). The directed-referral rule (§ 411.354(d)(4)) does not help. It permits an employer to *require* referrals within limits, through a written agreement with carve-outs for patient choice, insurer determination and medical judgment. It does not permit paying per referral.')
P('**Consequences.**')
B('**Stark.** Every Medicare DHS referral by an RQB-eligible employed physician to Greenfield since January 1, 2022 is prohibited unless another exception applies. The IOASE does not apply (Issue 2).')
B('**AKS.** A per-referral cash payment for referrals of federal program business, including to the ASC, is the paradigm AKS violation. The bona fide employee safe harbor (§ 1001.952(i)) does not protect payments for referrals as opposed to services. The memo’s stated purpose (“incentivize the care coordination practices…” and “strengthen the Greenfield network”) and the 2023 hotline complaint make intent hard to contest.')
B('**Scienter.** The program was designed and signed by the Managing Member and CFO. It was reviewed by the CCO in 2022 and again in 2023, each time without counsel, despite contrary language in Greenfield’s own employment agreements. Those facts support at least reckless disregard under the FCA.')
B('**Possible link to utilization.** Hotline #2023-13 (Oct. 25, 2023) reported a “standard panel” of ECG, lipid panel and BMP for all new cardiology patients. Four employed cardiologists received RQB payments, and in-house laboratory tests are qualifying referrals. The CCO’s medical-necessity review was limited (30 charts). Counsel should consider whether referral-driven ordering affected utilization.')
P('**Defense observations.** The relator overstates parts of Count I (see Part VI): the rate ($200 versus $150), the population (“all 87 physicians” versus employed physicians only), and “set in advance” and “writing” elements that the employment exception does not contain. None of these errors cures the core defect.')
H('Remediation', 3)
N('By Compensation Committee action under OA § 7.5(c) (“sole discretion to … suspend, or terminate”), with Dr. Stein and Dr. Narayan recused, **suspend the RQB immediately and stop all accrued and future payments.** Do not make the next quarterly payment. Communicate the change carefully and under counsel’s supervision. Instruct that physicians are not to be told to “make up” the lost income through referrals.')
N('Do not try to recharacterize past RQB payments as productivity or quality pay. Counsel should decide whether to seek repayment from physicians, considering the period-of-disallowance rules (§ 411.353(c)), employment-law constraints, and the effect on physicians who will be witnesses.')
N('Replace the RQB with compensation that complies with the exception:')
B('wRVU productivity for personally performed services, including “incident to” services only as § 411.352(i) permits;', 1)
B('quality metrics that are objective, verifiable and not referral-based (HEDIS gap closure, patient experience, documentation). Consider the value-based exceptions (§ 411.357(aa)) only with counsel and a documented value-based enterprise.', 1)
N('Obtain an **independent, current FMV and commercial-reasonableness opinion** on total employed-physician compensation before any new plan takes effect. Document the plan in signed amendments to each employment agreement.')
N('Amend the OA (two-thirds written vote, § 14.1) to delete § 7.5(c) and the “Qualified Internal Referral” definition. Determine when and how that language entered the January 1, 2020 OA.')
N('Quantify, under privilege, all RQB payments (2020 or 2022 forward) and the Medicare and Medicaid DHS claims tied to RQB recipients’ referrals. Feed the results into the disclosure analysis (Part VII).')

# ---------------- ISSUE 2
H('Issue 2 — The RQB Very Likely Destroys “Group Practice” Status, So the IOASE Fails for All Physicians (Critical)', 2)
H('Facts', 3)
P('Greenfield claims the IOASE for all in-house laboratory and imaging DHS billed under its group NPI (audit memo § III.A; OA § 10.2; Manual §§ 3.2.4, 5.1). The RQB is paid to the 31 employed physicians, who are “members of the group” under § 411.351. Member physicians receive Buckeye Referral Credits (Issue 5).')
H('Analysis', 3)
P('To be a “group practice”, a group must, among other things, ensure that “no physician who is a member of the group practice directly or indirectly receives compensation based on the volume or value of his or her referrals,” except as permitted for productivity bonuses and profit shares under § 411.352(i) (§ 411.352(g)). The RQB pays employed group members per DHS referral to the group’s own ancillaries. It is neither a productivity bonus for personally performed services nor an overall profit share. On the face of the regulation, Greenfield therefore did not qualify as a group practice for any period in which the RQB was in effect.')
P('The group-practice definition is a threshold for the IOASE (§ 411.355(b)(1)(ii), (b)(2)(ii), (b)(3)). Losing it has three consequences:')
B('the IOASE is unavailable to **every** referring physician, including the 52 members who never received the RQB;')
B('members’ ownership interests in Greenfield are then unprotected. No other exception covers ownership of a group that furnishes in-office laboratory and imaging services;')
B('the analysis applies to all Medicare (and, through § 1396b(s), Medicaid) laboratory and imaging DHS billed by Greenfield from January 1, 2022, and earlier if the RQB or a predecessor existed.')
P('This is potentially the largest single exposure in the file. The relator has not clearly pleaded it: Count I focuses on referrals “generated under” the RQB (Compl. ¶¶ 44–46). An amended complaint or the government could plead it. The 2023 figure of roughly $98.3 million in Medicare and Medicaid claims (Compl. ¶ 10) covers all services, most of which are not DHS (e.g., E/M visits and surgeons’ professional services). The DHS subset must be quantified.')
P('Possible arguments to narrow the exposure are limited and should be tested by counsel:')
B('**Employed physicians’ referrals.** Their compensation from their own employer may separately meet no exception, so the IOASE question matters mostly for members. Members do not receive the RQB, but group-practice status is assessed at the entity level.')
B('**Divisible periods.** Status may be restored prospectively once the RQB ends and any other § 411.352(g) issue is corrected.')
B('**Remedies.** The defect is structural. The 90-day special rule for reconciling compensation discrepancies (§ 411.353(h)) is unlikely to help.')
H('Remediation', 3)
N('Terminate the RQB (Issue 1). Remove the Buckeye Referral Credit from member compensation (Issue 5). Confirm that no other member compensation varies with DHS referrals.')
N('Document **overall-profits** and **productivity** methods that meet § 411.352(i), with supporting documentation kept as § 411.352(i)(4) requires. Have counsel certify that group-practice status has been restored, as of a stated date.')
N('Obtain Medicare and Medicaid DHS billing data by CPT, site and year (2019–present) to size the refund base. Model scenarios: all DHS, DHS ordered by RQB recipients only, and DHS by site.')
EOF
echo ok"

Stark-tainted claims are false without any intent showing for the underlying violation, but FCA liability requires that the claims be submitted \u201cknowingly\u201d (31 U.S.C. \u00a7 3729(b)(1)). Under 42 U.S.C. \u00a7 1320a-7k(d) and 42 C.F.R. \u00a7 401.305, an identified overpayment must be reported and returned within 60 days of identification, subject to the six-year lookback. The rule as amended effective January 1, 2025 allows up to 180 days of suspension for a timely, good-faith investigation. An overpayment that is retained becomes an FCA \u201creverse false claim\u201d (31 U.S.C. \u00a7 3729(a)(1)(G)).')

H('V. Analysis of Issues', 1)

# ---------------- ISSUE 1
H('Issue 1 \u2014 The \u201cReferral Quality Bonus\u201d Is a Per-Referral Payment That Defeats the Employment Exception (Critical)', 2)
H('Facts', 3)
B('The Compensation Plan Update Memorandum is dated January 10, 2022 and is signed by Dr. Stein and the CFO. It says the plan was approved by the Compensation Committee on December 14, 2021 and is effective January 1, 2022, i.e., retroactively. It pays every employed (non-member) physician **$150 per \u201cQualified Internal Referral\u201d**, calculated and paid quarterly, capped at **$90,000 per physician per year (600 referrals)** (\u00a7\u00a7 4.1\u20134.4).')
B('A \u201cQualified Internal Referral\u201d is a referral to (a) a Greenfield member or employed specialist, (b) Buckeye Surgical Center, or (c) **Greenfield\u2019s in-office ancillary services: clinical laboratory, point-of-care testing and diagnostic imaging** (\u00a7 4.2). The referral counts only if the service is **completed and billed** (\u00a7\u00a7 4.2, 5(c)). The billing department tracks referrals by category: specialist, Buckeye, ancillary (\u00a7 5).')
B('There is no quality component. Payment is triggered by the referral order, the patient\u2019s appearance and the billing of the service. Nothing in the memo measures clinical appropriateness, outcomes or guideline adherence. The memo\u2019s own rationale is to \u201ccompensat[e] physicians for each Qualified Internal Referral\u201d (\u00a7 4.5).')
B('The memo states that \u201c[n]o amendment to your individual employment agreement is required\u201d (\u00a7 7). The Wellford agreement, signed five days after the memo, does not mention the RQB:')
B('\u00a7 4.3 permits added compensation only by written amendment or by a plan \u201cconsistent with \u2026 42 U.S.C. \u00a7 1395nn\u201d;', 1)
B('\u00a7 4.6 prohibits any remuneration \u201cin connection with \u2026 Physician\u2019s referral of patients for designated health services\u201d;', 1)
B('Exhibit B describes base salary, productivity bonus and benefits as \u201call compensation payable.\u201d', 1)
B('OA \u00a7 7.5(c) authorizes the RQB \u201cto reward Employed Physicians who maintain robust referral networks.\u201d The OA is stated to be effective January 1, 2020, two years before the December 2021 approval, and also defines \u201cQualified Internal Referral.\u201d Either the OA was changed without the two-thirds written amendment that OA \u00a7 14.1 requires, or a referral-based bonus was contemplated (and possibly paid) before 2022. Either way, the look-back may need to start before 2022.')
B('**2023 payments:** $1,260,000 to 31 employed physicians, equal to **8,400 paid referrals**. Of that, $712,500 (57%) went to 12 internal-medicine physicians. Examples:')
B('Dr. Martinez was paid at the $90,000 cap;', 1)
B('Dr. Wellford received $78,000 (520 referrals). That is 27% of his $285,000 base and almost double his $42,000 productivity bonus.', 1)
B('The March 31, 2022 internal audit reviewed the RQB and found \u201c[n]o compliance concerns\u201d (\u00a7 V). Hotline report #2023-07 (Apr. 12, 2023) called the RQB \u201ca kickback for referrals.\u201d The CCO closed it in 16 days as \u201ca legitimate quality metric,\u201d with no Compliance Committee review and no counsel. That violated Manual \u00a7 6.3, Steps 3 and 6 (Committee notice within five business days for Stark/AKS reports; Committee review of findings).')
H('Analysis', 3)
P('**Employment exception fails.** Compensation that pays a fixed dollar amount for each referral uses referrals as a variable and rises with them. Under \u00a7 411.354(d)(5)(i) it \u201ctakes into account the volume or value of referrals\u201d per se. The RQB counts DHS referrals in two ways:')
B('directly, through referrals to Greenfield\u2019s in-house laboratory and imaging;')
B('indirectly, through referrals to Greenfield specialists. Under \u00a7 411.351, any test the consulting specialist orders is itself a referral by the requesting physician.')
P('No employed physician receiving the RQB can satisfy \u00a7 411.357(c)(4) (the volume/value standard), and the productivity carve-out applies only to personally performed services. The RQB is also not FMV for any identifiable service. It pays for the referral, not for work, and the only benchmarking study (Lakeshore, November 2019) predates the program and did not evaluate it (Compl. \u00b6 39; Comp. Memo \u00a7 1). The directed-referral rule (\u00a7 411.354(d)(4)) does not help. It permits an employer to *require* referrals within limits, through a written agreement with carve-outs for patient choice, insurer determination and medical judgment. It does not permit paying per referral.')
P('**Consequences.**')
B('**Stark.** Every Medicare DHS referral by an RQB-eligible employed physician to Greenfield since January 1, 2022 is prohibited unless another exception applies. The IOASE does not apply (Issue 2).')
B('**AKS.** A per-referral cash payment for referrals of federal program business, including to the ASC, is the paradigm AKS violation. The bona fide employee safe harbor (\u00a7 1001.952(i)) does not protect payments for referrals as opposed to services. The memo\u2019s stated purpose (\u201cincentivize the care coordination practices\u2026\u201d and \u201cstrengthen the Greenfield network\u201d) and the 2023 hotline complaint make intent hard to contest.')
B('**Scienter.** The program was designed and signed by the Managing Member and CFO. It was reviewed by the CCO in 2022 and again in 2023, each time without counsel, despite contrary language in Greenfield\u2019s own employment agreements. Those facts support at least reckless disregard under the FCA.')
B('**Possible link to utilization.** Hotline #2023-13 (Oct. 25, 2023) reported a \u201cstandard panel\u201d of ECG, lipid panel and BMP for all new cardiology patients. Four employed cardiologists received RQB payments, and in-house laboratory tests are qualifying referrals. The CCO\u2019s medical-necessity review was limited (30 charts). Counsel should consider whether referral-driven ordering affected utilization.')
P('**Defense observations.** The relator overstates parts of Count I (see Part VI): the rate ($200 versus $150), the population (\u201call 87 physicians\u201d versus employed physicians only), and \u201cset in advance\u201d and \u201cwriting\u201d elements that the employment exception does not contain. None of these errors cures the core defect.')
H('Remediation', 3)
N('By Compensation Committee action under OA \u00a7 7.5(c) (\u201csole discretion to \u2026 suspend, or terminate\u201d), with Dr. Stein and Dr. Narayan recused, **suspend the RQB immediately and stop all accrued and future payments.** Do not make the next quarterly payment. Communicate the change carefully and under counsel\u2019s supervision. Instruct that physicians are not to be told to \u201cmake up\u201d the lost income through referrals.')
N('Do not try to recharacterize past RQB payments as productivity or quality pay. Counsel should decide whether to seek repayment from physicians, considering the period-of-disallowance rules (\u00a7 411.353(c)), employment-law constraints, and the effect on physicians who will be witnesses.')
N('Replace the RQB with compensation that complies with the exception:')
B('wRVU productivity for personally performed services, including \u201cincident to\u201d services only as \u00a7 411.352(i) permits;', 1)
B('quality metrics that are objective, verifiable and not referral-based (HEDIS gap closure, patient experience, documentation). Consider the value-based exceptions (\u00a7 411.357(aa)) only with counsel and a documented value-based enterprise.', 1)
N('Obtain an **independent, current FMV and commercial-reasonableness opinion** on total employed-physician compensation before any new plan takes effect. Document the plan in signed amendments to each employment agreement.')
N('Amend the OA (two-thirds written vote, \u00a7 14.1) to delete \u00a7 7.5(c) and the \u201cQualified Internal Referral\u201d definition. Determine when and how that language entered the January 1, 2020 OA.')
N('Quantify, under privilege, all RQB payments (2020 or 2022 forward) and the Medicare and Medicaid DHS claims tied to RQB recipients\u2019 referrals. Feed the results into the disclosure analysis (Part VII).')

# ---------------- ISSUE 2
H('Issue 2 \u2014 The RQB Very Likely Destroys \u201cGroup Practice\u201d Status, So the IOASE Fails for All Physicians (Critical)', 2)
H('Facts', 3)
P('Greenfield claims the IOASE for all in-house laboratory and imaging DHS billed under its group NPI (audit memo \u00a7 III.A; OA \u00a7 10.2; Manual \u00a7\u00a7 3.2.4, 5.1). The RQB is paid to the 31 employed physicians, who are \u201cmembers of the group\u201d under \u00a7 411.351. Member physicians receive Buckeye Referral Credits (Issue 5).')
H('Analysis', 3)
P('To be a \u201cgroup practice\u201d, a group must, among other things, ensure that \u201cno physician who is a member of the group practice directly or indirectly receives compensation based on the volume or value of his or her referrals,\u201d except as permitted for productivity bonuses and profit shares under \u00a7 411.352(i) (\u00a7 411.352(g)). The RQB pays employed group members per DHS referral to the group\u2019s own ancillaries. It is neither a productivity bonus for personally performed services nor an overall profit share. On the face of the regulation, Greenfield therefore did not qualify as a group practice for any period in which the RQB was in effect.')
P('The group-practice definition is a threshold for the IOASE (\u00a7 411.355(b)(1)(ii), (b)(2)(ii), (b)(3)). Losing it has three consequences:')
B('the IOASE is unavailable to **every** referring physician, including the 52 members who never received the RQB;')
B('members\u2019 ownership interests in Greenfield are then unprotected. No other exception covers ownership of a group that furnishes in-office laboratory and imaging services;')
B('the analysis applies to all Medicare (and, through \u00a7 1396b(s), Medicaid) laboratory and imaging DHS billed by Greenfield from January 1, 2022, and earlier if the RQB or a predecessor existed.')
P('This is potentially the largest single exposure in the file. The relator has not clearly pleaded it: Count I focuses on referrals \u201cgenerated under\u201d the RQB (Compl. \u00b6\u00b6 44\u201346). An amended complaint or the government could plead it. The 2023 figure of roughly $98.3 million in Medicare and Medicaid claims (Compl. \u00b6 10) covers all services, most of which are not DHS (e.g., E/M visits and surgeons\u2019 professional services). The DHS subset must be quantified.')
P('Possible arguments to narrow the exposure are limited and should be tested by counsel:')
B('**Employed physicians\u2019 referrals.** Their compensation from their own employer may separately meet no exception, so the IOASE question matters mostly for members. Members do not receive the RQB, but group-practice status is assessed at the entity level.')
B('**Divisible periods.** Status may be restored prospectively once the RQB ends and any other \u00a7 411.352(g) issue is corrected.')
B('**Remedies.** The defect is structural. The 90-day special rule for reconciling compensation discrepancies (\u00a7 411.353(h)) is unlikely to help.')
H('Remediation', 3)
N('Terminate the RQB (Issue 1). Remove the Buckeye Referral Credit from member compensation (Issue 5). Confirm that no other member compensation varies with DHS referrals.')
N('Document **overall-profits** and **productivity** methods that meet \u00a7 411.352(i), with supporting documentation kept as \u00a7 411.352(i)(4) requires. Have counsel certify that group-practice status has been restored, as of a stated date.')
N('Obtain Medicare and Medicaid DHS billing data by CPT, site and year (2019\u2013present) to size the refund base. Model scenarios: all DHS, DHS ordered by RQB recipients only, and DHS by site.')
EOF
echo ok"

/home/user/Lawless_Research_Lab/harvey_lab/sbx.sh /home/user/Lawless_Research_Lab/harvey_lab/vendor/harvey-labs/results/healthcare-life-sciences/identify-stark-law-compliance-issues/claude-code-session/20261015-115344 "cat > /workspace/part3.py <<'EOF'
# ---------------- ISSUE 3
H('Issue 3 — Pinnacle Reference Laboratory Lease: Below FMV, Stale and Misdescribed Appraisal (High)', 2)
H('Facts', 3)
B('**Space and term.** Suite 105, 1,800 sf, March 1, 2022 to February 28, 2025. The lease has no renewal or holdover provision.')
B('**Rent.** Base rent is **$22.00/sf ($39,600/yr)**, fixed with no escalation (§§ 3.1, 3.3). The tenant pays only its share of *increases* in taxes and operating expenses over a 2022 base year (§ 3.4). In substance this is a modified-gross lease. The landlord also supplies HVAC, water, sewer, trash, common-area maintenance and five-day janitorial service (§§ 5.1, 5.3).')
B('**Appraisal.** The Lakeshore appraisal, by David Cho, MAI, ASA, concluded **$28–$32/sf on a full-service-gross (FSG) basis** as of September 1, 2020. It advised that any lease executed more than 12 months after that date should be supported by an update (transmittal letter; § 7). The Pinnacle lease was signed about 18 months after the value date. No update was obtained.')
B('**Suite-specific analysis.** The appraisal priced Suite 105 at **$50,400–$57,600/yr**. It noted that existing lab-suitable plumbing “may support upper end of range due to reduced TI burden.”')
B('**Misdescription of the appraisal.** The lease’s Exhibit B summary of the appraisal states the conclusion on a “**triple-net equivalent basis**” and describes the methodology as “sales comparison approach and income approach.” Both are inaccurate. The appraisal is FSG, and it relied primarily on market rent comparables, using sales comparison only as a check. The lease nonetheless recites that rent was “established with reference to” the appraisal (§ 3.2) and that the parties relied on it for FMV (§ 10.3).')
B('**Arm’s-length recital.** Section 3.6 recites “arm’s-length negotiation between unrelated parties.” Pinnacle’s CEO is Sandra Cho; the appraiser is David Cho. We have no evidence of any relationship, and the shared surname may be coincidental. It should be checked because it affects the appraisal’s independence and the § 3.6 representation.')
B('**Referral dependence.** Greenfield physicians are the source of about 55% of Pinnacle’s specimen volume. Greenfield is Pinnacle’s largest referral source (courier workbook, Notes tab; Compl. ¶ 64).')
B('**Management’s explanation.** Management attributed the rate to “tenant improvement credits and market conditions” (audit memo § IV). The lease contains no TI credit; the premises were taken “as-is” (§ 2.3).')
H('Analysis', 3)
P('Pinnacle furnishes clinical laboratory DHS. Under the stand-in-the-shoes rule, each Greenfield owner has a direct compensation arrangement with Pinnacle through the lease. The rental of office space exception therefore must be met for any Greenfield owner’s Medicare referral to Pinnacle. The writing, term and premises elements appear to be satisfied, subject to confirming fully executed copies; the file copies show blank signature lines. The **FMV element fails on the record**:')
B('a modified-gross rent of $22/sf against a $28–$32/sf FSG range is **$6–$10/sf (21–31%) below market**;')
B('that is **$10,800–$18,000 per year**, or **$32,400–$54,000 over the term**, before any upward adjustment for the lab-ready suite or for market growth from 2020 to 2022, which the appraisal put at 2.5–3% per year pre-pandemic.')
P('Commercial reasonableness and the “not determined in a manner that takes into account referrals” element are also at risk. Below-market rent to a tenant that depends on the landlord’s referrals, together with free courier services (Issue 4), invites the inference that the discount reflects referrals. The Exhibit B misdescription will be cited as evidence of knowledge.')
P('**Who bears the Stark consequence.** The denial-of-payment and refund consequences fall on **Pinnacle**, the DHS entity that bills Medicare for the tests. Greenfield’s exposure is derivative but real:')
B('FCA “causing” liability (31 U.S.C. § 3729(a)(1)(A)–(B));')
B('the AKS, because below-FMV rent to a referral recipient is classic remuneration and the space rental safe harbor (§ 1001.952(b)) requires FMV;')
B('Stark CMPs if a circumvention scheme is found.')
P('The lease expired February 28, 2025 with no holdover clause. If Pinnacle has continued in occupancy, the holdover protection in § 411.357(a)(7) applies only if the holdover is on the same terms and the arrangement otherwise met the exception, which it did not.')
H('Remediation', 3)
N('Determine Pinnacle’s current occupancy status and the rent paid since March 1, 2025.')
N('Commission a **new, independent FMV appraisal**, gross and net, with an appraiser independent of Lakeshore (given the surname question). Enter a new signed lease of at least one year at FMV, with a valid holdover clause, approved by an unconflicted body.')
N('Do not attempt to collect retroactive “catch-up” rent outside a counsel-directed disclosure, because a unilateral true-up can be characterized as an admission without curing the past period. Quantify the historical shortfall for the disclosure analysis.')
N('Investigate any relationship between Sandra Cho and David Cho, and how the Exhibit B summary was prepared and by whom.')
N('Coordinate with Pinnacle through counsel. Pinnacle is the billing entity, faces its own refund exposure, and may be a witness or a co-subject.')

# ---------------- ISSUE 4
H('Issue 4 — Free Courier Services from Pinnacle to All 12 Greenfield Locations (High)', 2)
H('Facts', 3)
P('Greenfield Operations tracked 2,897 specimen pickups by Pinnacle in 2023 across all 12 Greenfield locations, including the 8 with Greenfield’s own in-office laboratories. Pinnacle sent **no invoices** in 2023 or any prior period. Greenfield estimates the service at $4,200 per month, or **$50,400 per year**, based on an informal Q1 2022 quote. There is **no written agreement**, and the lease does not mention the service. Operations believes the arrangement began about when Pinnacle moved in (early 2022). The workbook itself describes the service as provided “at no charge per informal arrangement” and the value as “unreimbursed.” The Compliance Manual lists “[f]ree courier services, specimen pick-up, or delivery services” as remuneration and prohibits in-kind benefits without a written FMV agreement (§ 4.2).')
H('Analysis', 3)
P('The legal character of the service turns on **what the courier carries and for whom**.')
B('A laboratory that collects specimens it will itself test, solely to perform its own service, is generally not viewed as conferring independent value on the referring physician. The Stark definition of remuneration also excludes items, devices and supplies used solely to collect, transport, process or store specimens for the entity furnishing them (§ 411.351).')
B('That exclusion covers **items**, not services. Government guidance has long treated courier services that do more than transport the lab’s own specimens as suspect: carrying specimens to other labs, moving specimens or records between the physician’s offices, delivering supplies, or relieving the practice of its own transport costs.')
P('Greenfield runs in-house laboratories at 8 sites. Daily pickups at all 12 sites therefore raise a real question whether Pinnacle’s couriers also move Greenfield’s own specimens (for example, from satellite sites without labs to Greenfield’s in-house labs), records or supplies. If they do, the service is remuneration from a DHS entity to Greenfield. No exception applies to an unwritten, no-charge service arrangement, so each owner’s Pinnacle referrals would be prohibited. This would be independent of the lease defect, and the AKS problem would be stronger still. Greenfield’s own description of the value as “unreimbursed” is unhelpful.')
H('Remediation', 3)
N('Under privilege, interview Operations and site managers and obtain Pinnacle route manifests to establish the scope of the courier service. Determine whether any non-Pinnacle specimens, inter-office transfers, records or supplies were carried.')
N('If the service is limited to Pinnacle-tested specimens, document that in a written protocol signed by both parties. If it is broader, either end the non-Pinnacle uses or have Greenfield pay FMV under a signed services agreement.')
N('Quantify any non-exempt value (about $4,200 per month is the internal estimate) for the disclosure analysis. Treat Issues 3 and 4 together as the “Pinnacle relationship.”')

# ---------------- ISSUE 5
H('Issue 5 — Buckeye Surgical Center: Referral-Based Distributions and the Greenfield “Referral Credit” (Critical under AKS; Medium under Stark)', 2)
H('Facts', 3)
B('**Buckeye level.** The Buckeye OA allocates net profits and losses “exclusively” by each member’s **Referral Percentage**, “not … in proportion to Membership Interests” (§ 4.1(a)–(b)). It distributes cash quarterly the same way (§ 4.2), as well as released reserves (§ 4.4). Referral Percentage is each member’s share of surgical cases referred to the Center. For Greenfield, that means cases referred by its physicians (§§ 1.9, 1.25–1.26).')
B('**Monitoring.** Greenfield, as Manager, tracks referrals, and members must report referral data (§§ 4.2(b), 6.2).')
B('**Utilization.** Physician members must “use commercially reasonable efforts … to utilize the Center” (§ 6.1). This sits awkwardly beside § 5.5(b), which disclaims any referral requirement “provided, however, that distributions … shall be allocated based on Referral Percentage.”')
B('**Greenfield’s representation.** In the Buckeye OA, Greenfield represented that it would pass Buckeye distributions to referring physicians through a “referral credit” (§ 4.5).')
B('**Greenfield level.** Under the Greenfield OA, Greenfield’s Buckeye returns are allocated first as **Referral Credits** equal to **0.5% of the facility fee revenue of each case a member refers to Buckeye**. Only the remainder is distributed pro rata (§ 8.4(b)). The credit is said to “align Member incentives with the success of the Company’s affiliated surgical center.”')
B('**2023 Referral Credits:** $36,900 on 900 cases at an average $8,200 facility fee. Dr. Stein received $14,022 on 342 cases.')
B('**Employed physicians.** Separately, they earn $150 RQB payments for Buckeye referrals (Issue 1).')
B('**Medical directorship.** Dr. Stein, a 25% personal owner, is also Buckeye’s paid Medical Director (Issue 6).')
B('**Contradictory internal statements.** The January 2022 Compensation Plan memo tells physicians that member profit distributions are “ownership-proportional and are not allocated on the basis of referral activity” (§ 6). The 2023 compensation notes repeat that statement (citing OA § 8.1). Both are contradicted by OA § 8.4 and by the Referral Credit column in the same workbook.')
H('Analysis', 3)
P('**Stark.** The relator alleges that the surgical procedures are DHS (Compl. ¶¶ 73, 87). That is wrong as a general matter. ASC facility services paid under the ASC payment system are excluded from the DHS definition (§ 411.351), so ownership of Buckeye is not, by itself, an ownership interest in a DHS entity. Count III’s Stark theory is therefore weak, and its “group practice” citation to § 411.352(i) concerns profit shares from the group’s DHS, not ASC returns. The Stark spillover risks are narrower:')
B('if Buckeye bills any items or services outside the ASC composite rate that are DHS (e.g., certain separately paid drugs, prosthetics or DME), referral-based distributions would implicate Stark directly;')
B('member compensation from Greenfield that turns on referrals to an affiliate gives the government a § 411.352(g) argument, because Referral Credits are part of member “compensation” from the group. It is also poor optics for any claim that Greenfield’s compensation design is referral-neutral.')
P('These points must be confirmed with Buckeye’s claims data.')
P('**AKS (the principal exposure).** Returns on investment tied to the investor’s referrals are a central concern of the AKS. The ASC safe harbor (§ 1001.952(r)) requires, among other things, that returns be **directly proportional to capital invested**. It also contains investor-qualification, “one-third” income and practice tests, and requires that investors not be required or encouraged to refer. The Buckeye OA does the opposite in express terms: it makes referrals the *exclusive* measure of return and imposes a utilization covenant. Greenfield’s 0.5%-per-case credit converts each referral into a traceable personal payment, with the CFO tracking cases and reporting them quarterly (OA § 8.4(c)). These provisions have been in place since 2016 (Buckeye) and since at least 2020 (Greenfield). Buckeye’s Medicare and Medicaid facility claims for patients referred by Greenfield physicians are at risk as AKS-tainted FCA claims. The relator alleges about $16.8 million in Medicare and Medicaid revenue for Buckeye in 2023 (Compl. ¶ 11). Ohio fee-splitting and related professional-conduct provisions (Ohio Rev. Code Chapter 4731) should also be reviewed.')
P('**Ownership records do not reconcile.** The Buckeye OA (never amended; transfers need the consent of all members, § 8.1) shows only three members: Greenfield 60%, Stein 25%, Narayan 15%. The 2023 compensation summary instead reports Buckeye ownership percentages for some 30 other Greenfield members, e.g., Adler 5.0%, Castillo 4.5%, Banerjee 4.0%. With Stein’s 25% and Narayan’s 15%, individual percentages total **113.5%**. Possible explanations:')
B('look-through attributions of Greenfield’s 60%, although those would not total 73.5%;')
B('undocumented transfers;')
B('data errors.')
P('Each has different AKS consequences, and the figures must be reconciled. The 900 credited cases are attributed entirely to 14 member physicians, while the relator alleges 702 Greenfield-referred cases (78%). The Buckeye OA’s “hypothetical” illustration uses exactly 702/342/56, and 342 is Dr. Stein’s actual 2023 count. This tends to undercut the label “hypothetical” and will be used to show that the drafters modeled actual referrals.')
H('Remediation', 3)
N('**Immediately suspend** Referral Credit allocations (OA § 8.4(b)). Hold Greenfield’s Buckeye returns in a segregated account pending counsel’s advice.')
N('Amend the **Buckeye OA** (all-member written consent, § 12.2(b)) so that allocations and distributions are strictly pro rata to capital and Membership Interests. Delete §§ 1.9, 1.25, 1.26, 4.5 and 6.2 and the utilization covenant in § 6.1. Restructure toward the ASC safe harbor, recognizing that a hospital-free, multispecialty, group-practice-investor ASC must meet the specific investor and income tests in § 1001.952(r).')
N('Amend the **Greenfield OA** (two-thirds vote) to delete § 8.4(b) and the Referral Credit definition, and to distribute Buckeye returns by Membership Interest. Correct the inaccurate statements in the 2022 Compensation memo.')
N('Reconcile Buckeye’s capitalization and ownership history. Obtain capital-contribution records (redacted in Ex. A) and all distribution statements since 2016. Determine whether any DHS is billed by Buckeye.')
N('Evaluate an **OIG Self-Disclosure Protocol** submission for the Buckeye conduct, coordinated with the overall strategy (Part VII). The CMS SRDP covers only Stark and is not the right vehicle for AKS conduct.')
N('Advise Dr. Stein and Dr. Narayan to retain **separate counsel**. They are named defendants and personally received referral-based Buckeye distributions.')
EOF
echo ok"

B('**Appraisal.** The Lakeshore appraisal, by David Cho, MAI, ASA, concluded **$28\u2013$32/sf on a full-service-gross (FSG) basis** as of September 1, 2020. It advised that any lease executed more than 12 months after that date should be supported by an update (transmittal letter; \u00a7 7). The Pinnacle lease was signed about 18 months after the value date. No update was obtained.')
B('**Suite-specific analysis.** The appraisal priced Suite 105 at **$50,400\u2013$57,600/yr**. It noted that existing lab-suitable plumbing \u201cmay support upper end of range due to reduced TI burden.\u201d')
B('**Misdescription of the appraisal.** The lease\u2019s Exhibit B summary of the appraisal states the conclusion on a \u201c**triple-net equivalent basis**\u201d and describes the methodology as \u201csales comparison approach and income approach.\u201d Both are inaccurate. The appraisal is FSG, and it relied primarily on market rent comparables, using sales comparison only as a check. The lease nonetheless recites that rent was \u201cestablished with reference to\u201d the appraisal (\u00a7 3.2) and that the parties relied on it for FMV (\u00a7 10.3).')
B('**Arm\u2019s-length recital.** Section 3.6 recites \u201carm\u2019s-length negotiation between unrelated parties.\u201d Pinnacle\u2019s CEO is Sandra Cho; the appraiser is David Cho. We have no evidence of any relationship, and the shared surname may be coincidental. It should be checked because it affects the appraisal\u2019s independence and the \u00a7 3.6 representation.')
B('**Referral dependence.** Greenfield physicians are the source of about 55% of Pinnacle\u2019s specimen volume. Greenfield is Pinnacle\u2019s largest referral source (courier workbook, Notes tab; Compl. \u00b6 64).')
B('**Management\u2019s explanation.** Management attributed the rate to \u201ctenant improvement credits and market conditions\u201d (audit memo \u00a7 IV). The lease contains no TI credit; the premises were taken \u201cas-is\u201d (\u00a7 2.3).')
H('Analysis', 3)
P('Pinnacle furnishes clinical laboratory DHS. Under the stand-in-the-shoes rule, each Greenfield owner has a direct compensation arrangement with Pinnacle through the lease. The rental of office space exception therefore must be met for any Greenfield owner\u2019s Medicare referral to Pinnacle. The writing, term and premises elements appear to be satisfied, subject to confirming fully executed copies; the file copies show blank signature lines. The **FMV element fails on the record**:')
B('a modified-gross rent of $22/sf against a $28\u2013$32/sf FSG range is **$6\u2013$10/sf (21\u201331%) below market**;')
B('that is **$10,800\u2013$18,000 per year**, or **$32,400\u2013$54,000 over the term**, before any upward adjustment for the lab-ready suite or for market growth from 2020 to 2022, which the appraisal put at 2.5\u20133% per year pre-pandemic.')
P('Commercial reasonableness and the \u201cnot determined in a manner that takes into account referrals\u201d element are also at risk. Below-market rent to a tenant that depends on the landlord\u2019s referrals, together with free courier services (Issue 4), invites the inference that the discount reflects referrals. The Exhibit B misdescription will be cited as evidence of knowledge.')
P('**Who bears the Stark consequence.** The denial-of-payment and refund consequences fall on **Pinnacle**, the DHS entity that bills Medicare for the tests. Greenfield\u2019s exposure is derivative but real:')
B('FCA \u201ccausing\u201d liability (31 U.S.C. \u00a7 3729(a)(1)(A)\u2013(B));')
B('the AKS, because below-FMV rent to a referral recipient is classic remuneration and the space rental safe harbor (\u00a7 1001.952(b)) requires FMV;')
B('Stark CMPs if a circumvention scheme is found.')
P('The lease expired February 28, 2025 with no holdover clause. If Pinnacle has continued in occupancy, the holdover protection in \u00a7 411.357(a)(7) applies only if the holdover is on the same terms and the arrangement otherwise met the exception, which it did not.')
H('Remediation', 3)
N('Determine Pinnacle\u2019s current occupancy status and the rent paid since March 1, 2025.')
N('Commission a **new, independent FMV appraisal**, gross and net, with an appraiser independent of Lakeshore (given the surname question). Enter a new signed lease of at least one year at FMV, with a valid holdover clause, approved by an unconflicted body.')
N('Do not attempt to collect retroactive \u201ccatch-up\u201d rent outside a counsel-directed disclosure, because a unilateral true-up can be characterized as an admission without curing the past period. Quantify the historical shortfall for the disclosure analysis.')
N('Investigate any relationship between Sandra Cho and David Cho, and how the Exhibit B summary was prepared and by whom.')
N('Coordinate with Pinnacle through counsel. Pinnacle is the billing entity, faces its own refund exposure, and may be a witness or a co-subject.')

# ---------------- ISSUE 4
H('Issue 4 \u2014 Free Courier Services from Pinnacle to All 12 Greenfield Locations (High)', 2)
H('Facts', 3)
P('Greenfield Operations tracked 2,897 specimen pickups by Pinnacle in 2023 across all 12 Greenfield locations, including the 8 with Greenfield\u2019s own in-office laboratories. Pinnacle sent **no invoices** in 2023 or any prior period. Greenfield estimates the service at $4,200 per month, or **$50,400 per year**, based on an informal Q1 2022 quote. There is **no written agreement**, and the lease does not mention the service. Operations believes the arrangement began about when Pinnacle moved in (early 2022). The workbook itself describes the service as provided \u201cat no charge per informal arrangement\u201d and the value as \u201cunreimbursed.\u201d The Compliance Manual lists \u201c[f]ree courier services, specimen pick-up, or delivery services\u201d as remuneration and prohibits in-kind benefits without a written FMV agreement (\u00a7 4.2).')
H('Analysis', 3)
P('The legal character of the service turns on **what the courier carries and for whom**.')
B('A laboratory that collects specimens it will itself test, solely to perform its own service, is generally not viewed as conferring independent value on the referring physician. The Stark definition of remuneration also excludes items, devices and supplies used solely to collect, transport, process or store specimens for the entity furnishing them (\u00a7 411.351).')
B('That exclusion covers **items**, not services. Government guidance has long treated courier services that do more than transport the lab\u2019s own specimens as suspect: carrying specimens to other labs, moving specimens or records between the physician\u2019s offices, delivering supplies, or relieving the practice of its own transport costs.')
P('Greenfield runs in-house laboratories at 8 sites. Daily pickups at all 12 sites therefore raise a real question whether Pinnacle\u2019s couriers also move Greenfield\u2019s own specimens (for example, from satellite sites without labs to Greenfield\u2019s in-house labs), records or supplies. If they do, the service is remuneration from a DHS entity to Greenfield. No exception applies to an unwritten, no-charge service arrangement, so each owner\u2019s Pinnacle referrals would be prohibited. This would be independent of the lease defect, and the AKS problem would be stronger still. Greenfield\u2019s own description of the value as \u201cunreimbursed\u201d is unhelpful.')
H('Remediation', 3)
N('Under privilege, interview Operations and site managers and obtain Pinnacle route manifests to establish the scope of the courier service. Determine whether any non-Pinnacle specimens, inter-office transfers, records or supplies were carried.')
N('If the service is limited to Pinnacle-tested specimens, document that in a written protocol signed by both parties. If it is broader, either end the non-Pinnacle uses or have Greenfield pay FMV under a signed services agreement.')
N('Quantify any non-exempt value (about $4,200 per month is the internal estimate) for the disclosure analysis. Treat Issues 3 and 4 together as the \u201cPinnacle relationship.\u201d')

# ---------------- ISSUE 5
H('Issue 5 \u2014 Buckeye Surgical Center: Referral-Based Distributions and the Greenfield \u201cReferral Credit\u201d (Critical under AKS; Medium under Stark)', 2)
H('Facts', 3)
B('**Buckeye level.** The Buckeye OA allocates net profits and losses \u201cexclusively\u201d by each member\u2019s **Referral Percentage**, \u201cnot \u2026 in proportion to Membership Interests\u201d (\u00a7 4.1(a)\u2013(b)). It distributes cash quarterly the same way (\u00a7 4.2), as well as released reserves (\u00a7 4.4). Referral Percentage is each member\u2019s share of surgical cases referred to the Center. For Greenfield, that means cases referred by its physicians (\u00a7\u00a7 1.9, 1.25\u20131.26).')
B('**Monitoring.** Greenfield, as Manager, tracks referrals, and members must report referral data (\u00a7\u00a7 4.2(b), 6.2).')
B('**Utilization.** Physician members must \u201cuse commercially reasonable efforts \u2026 to utilize the Center\u201d (\u00a7 6.1). This sits awkwardly beside \u00a7 5.5(b), which disclaims any referral requirement \u201cprovided, however, that distributions \u2026 shall be allocated based on Referral Percentage.\u201d')
B('**Greenfield\u2019s representation.** In the Buckeye OA, Greenfield represented that it would pass Buckeye distributions to referring physicians through a \u201creferral credit\u201d (\u00a7 4.5).')
B('**Greenfield level.** Under the Greenfield OA, Greenfield\u2019s Buckeye returns are allocated first as **Referral Credits** equal to **0.5% of the facility fee revenue of each case a member refers to Buckeye**. Only the remainder is distributed pro rata (\u00a7 8.4(b)). The credit is said to \u201calign Member incentives with the success of the Company\u2019s affiliated surgical center.\u201d')
B('**2023 Referral Credits:** $36,900 on 900 cases at an average $8,200 facility fee. Dr. Stein received $14,022 on 342 cases.')
B('**Employed physicians.** Separately, they earn $150 RQB payments for Buckeye referrals (Issue 1).')
B('**Medical directorship.** Dr. Stein, a 25% personal owner, is also Buckeye\u2019s paid Medical Director (Issue 6).')
B('**Contradictory internal statements.** The January 2022 Compensation Plan memo tells physicians that member profit distributions are \u201cownership-proportional and are not allocated on the basis of referral activity\u201d (\u00a7 6). The 2023 compensation notes repeat that statement (citing OA \u00a7 8.1). Both are contradicted by OA \u00a7 8.4 and by the Referral Credit column in the same workbook.')
H('Analysis', 3)
P('**Stark.** The relator alleges that the surgical procedures are DHS (Compl. \u00b6\u00b6 73, 87). That is wrong as a general matter. ASC facility services paid under the ASC payment system are excluded from the DHS definition (\u00a7 411.351), so ownership of Buckeye is not, by itself, an ownership interest in a DHS entity. Count III\u2019s Stark theory is therefore weak, and its \u201cgroup practice\u201d citation to \u00a7 411.352(i) concerns profit shares from the group\u2019s DHS, not ASC returns. The Stark spillover risks are narrower:')
B('if Buckeye bills any items or services outside the ASC composite rate that are DHS (e.g., certain separately paid drugs, prosthetics or DME), referral-based distributions would implicate Stark directly;')
B('member compensation from Greenfield that turns on referrals to an affiliate gives the government a \u00a7 411.352(g) argument, because Referral Credits are part of member \u201ccompensation\u201d from the group. It is also poor optics for any claim that Greenfield\u2019s compensation design is referral-neutral.')
P('These points must be confirmed with Buckeye\u2019s claims data.')
P('**AKS (the principal exposure).** Returns on investment tied to the investor\u2019s referrals are a central concern of the AKS. The ASC safe harbor (\u00a7 1001.952(r)) requires, among other things, that returns be **directly proportional to capital invested**. It also contains investor-qualification, \u201cone-third\u201d income and practice tests, and requires that investors not be required or encouraged to refer. The Buckeye OA does the opposite in express terms: it makes referrals the *exclusive* measure of return and imposes a utilization covenant. Greenfield\u2019s 0.5%-per-case credit converts each referral into a traceable personal payment, with the CFO tracking cases and reporting them quarterly (OA \u00a7 8.4(c)). These provisions have been in place since 2016 (Buckeye) and since at least 2020 (Greenfield). Buckeye\u2019s Medicare and Medicaid facility claims for patients referred by Greenfield physicians are at risk as AKS-tainted FCA claims. The relator alleges about $16.8 million in Medicare and Medicaid revenue for Buckeye in 2023 (Compl. \u00b6 11). Ohio fee-splitting and related professional-conduct provisions (Ohio Rev. Code Chapter 4731) should also be reviewed.')
P('**Ownership records do not reconcile.** The Buckeye OA (never amended; transfers need the consent of all members, \u00a7 8.1) shows only three members: Greenfield 60%, Stein 25%, Narayan 15%. The 2023 compensation summary instead reports Buckeye ownership percentages for some 30 other Greenfield members, e.g., Adler 5.0%, Castillo 4.5%, Banerjee 4.0%. With Stein\u2019s 25% and Narayan\u2019s 15%, individual percentages total **113.5%**. Possible explanations:')
B('look-through attributions of Greenfield\u2019s 60%, although those would not total 73.5%;')
B('undocumented transfers;')
B('data errors.')
P('Each has different AKS consequences, and the figures must be reconciled. The 900 credited cases are attributed entirely to 14 member physicians, while the relator alleges 702 Greenfield-referred cases (78%). The Buckeye OA\u2019s \u201chypothetical\u201d illustration uses exactly 702/342/56, and 342 is Dr. Stein\u2019s actual 2023 count. This tends to undercut the label \u201chypothetical\u201d and will be used to show that the drafters modeled actual referrals.')
H('Remediation', 3)
N('**Immediately suspend** Referral Credit allocations (OA \u00a7 8.4(b)). Hold Greenfield\u2019s Buckeye returns in a segregated account pending counsel\u2019s advice.')
N('Amend the **Buckeye OA** (all-member written consent, \u00a7 12.2(b)) so that allocations and distributions are strictly pro rata to capital and Membership Interests. Delete \u00a7\u00a7 1.9, 1.25, 1.26, 4.5 and 6.2 and the utilization covenant in \u00a7 6.1. Restructure toward the ASC safe harbor, recognizing that a hospital-free, multispecialty, group-practice-investor ASC must meet the specific investor and income tests in \u00a7 1001.952(r).')
N('Amend the **Greenfield OA** (two-thirds vote) to delete \u00a7 8.4(b) and the Referral Credit definition, and to distribute Buckeye returns by Membership Interest. Correct the inaccurate statements in the 2022 Compensation memo.')
N('Reconcile Buckeye\u2019s capitalization and ownership history. Obtain capital-contribution records (redacted in Ex. A) and all distribution statements since 2016. Determine whether any DHS is billed by Buckeye.')
N('Evaluate an **OIG Self-Disclosure Protocol** submission for the Buckeye conduct, coordinated with the overall strategy (Part VII). The CMS SRDP covers only Stark and is not the right vehicle for AKS conduct.')
N('Advise Dr. Stein and Dr. Narayan to retain **separate counsel**. They are named defendants and personally received referral-based Buckeye distributions.')
EOF
echo ok"
