H('Issue 3 — Pinnacle Reference Laboratory Lease: Below FMV, Stale and Misdescribed Appraisal (High)', 2)
H('Facts', 3)
B('**Space and term.** Suite 105, 1,800 sf, March 1, 2022 to February 28, 2025. The lease has no renewal or holdover provision.')
B('**Rent.** Base rent is **\$22.00/sf (\$39,600/yr)**, fixed with no escalation (§§ 3.1, 3.3). The tenant pays only its share of *increases* in taxes and operating expenses over a 2022 base year (§ 3.4). In substance this is a modified-gross lease. The landlord also supplies HVAC, water, sewer, trash, common-area maintenance and five-day janitorial service (§§ 5.1, 5.3).')
B('**Appraisal.** The Lakeshore appraisal, by David Cho, MAI, ASA, concluded **\$28–\$32/sf on a full-service-gross (FSG) basis** as of September 1, 2020. It advised that any lease executed more than 12 months after that date should be supported by an update (transmittal letter; § 7). The Pinnacle lease was signed about 18 months after the value date. No update was obtained.')
B('**Suite-specific analysis.** The appraisal priced Suite 105 at **\$50,400–\$57,600/yr**. It noted that existing lab-suitable plumbing “may support upper end of range due to reduced TI burden.”')
B('**Misdescription of the appraisal.** The lease’s Exhibit B summary of the appraisal states the conclusion on a “**triple-net equivalent basis**” and describes the methodology as “sales comparison approach and income approach.” Both are inaccurate. The appraisal is FSG, and it relied primarily on market rent comparables, using sales comparison only as a check. The lease nonetheless recites that rent was “established with reference to” the appraisal (§ 3.2) and that the parties relied on it for FMV (§ 10.3).')
B('**Arm’s-length recital.** Section 3.6 recites “arm’s-length negotiation between unrelated parties.” Pinnacle’s CEO is Sandra Cho; the appraiser is David Cho. We have no evidence of any relationship, and the shared surname may be coincidental. It should be checked because it affects the appraisal’s independence and the § 3.6 representation.')
B('**Referral dependence.** Greenfield physicians are the source of about 55% of Pinnacle’s specimen volume. Greenfield is Pinnacle’s largest referral source (courier workbook, Notes tab; Compl. ¶ 64).')
B('**Management’s explanation.** Management attributed the rate to “tenant improvement credits and market conditions” (audit memo § IV). The lease contains no TI credit; the premises were taken “as-is” (§ 2.3).')
H('Analysis', 3)
P('Pinnacle furnishes clinical laboratory DHS. Under the stand-in-the-shoes rule, each Greenfield owner has a direct compensation arrangement with Pinnacle through the lease. The rental of office space exception therefore must be met for any Greenfield owner’s Medicare referral to Pinnacle. The writing, term and premises elements appear to be satisfied, subject to confirming fully executed copies; the file copies show blank signature lines. The **FMV element fails on the record**:')
B('a modified-gross rent of \$22/sf against a \$28–\$32/sf FSG range is **\$6–\$10/sf (21–31%) below market**;')
B('that is **\$10,800–\$18,000 per year**, or **\$32,400–\$54,000 over the term**, before any upward adjustment for the lab-ready suite or for market growth from 2020 to 2022, which the appraisal put at 2.5–3% per year pre-pandemic.')
P('Commercial reasonableness and the “not determined in a manner that takes into account referrals” element are also at risk. Below-market rent to a tenant that depends on the landlord’s referrals, together with free courier services (Issue 4), invites the inference that the discount reflects referrals. The Exhibit B misdescription will be cited as evidence of knowledge.')
P('**Who bears the Stark consequence.** The denial-of-payment and refund consequences fall on **Pinnacle**, the DHS entity that bills Medicare for the tests. Greenfield’s exposure is derivative but real:')
B('FCA “causing” liability (31 U.S.C. § 3729(a)(1)(A)–(B));')
B('the AKS, because below-FMV rent to a referral recipient is classic remuneration and the space rental safe harbor (§ 1001.952(b)) requires FMV;')
B('Stark CMPs if a circumvention scheme is found.')
P('The lease expired February 28, 2025 with no holdover clause. If Pinnacle has continued in occupancy, the holdover protection in § 411.357(a)(7) applies only if the holdover is on the same terms and the arrangement otherwise met the exception, which it did not.')
H('Remediation', 3)
N('Determine Pinnacle’s current occupancy status and the rent paid since March 1, 2025.')
N('Commission a **new, independent FMV appraisal**, gross and net, with an appraiser independent of Lakeshore (given the surname question). Enter a new signed lease of at least one year at FMV, with a valid holdover clause, approved by an unconflicted body.')
N('Do not attempt to collect retroactive “catch-up” rent outside a counsel-directed disclosure, because a unilateral true-up can be characterized as an admission without curing the past period. Quantify the historical shortfall for the disclosure analysis.')
N('Investigate any relationship between Sandra Cho and David Cho, and how the Exhibit B summary was prepared and by whom.')
N('Coordinate with Pinnacle through counsel. Pinnacle is the billing entity, faces its own refund exposure, and may be a witness or a co-subject.')

H('Issue 4 — Free Courier Services from Pinnacle to All 12 Greenfield Locations (High)', 2)
H('Facts', 3)
P('Greenfield Operations tracked 2,897 specimen pickups by Pinnacle in 2023 across all 12 Greenfield locations, including the 8 with Greenfield’s own in-office laboratories. Pinnacle sent **no invoices** in 2023 or any prior period. Greenfield estimates the service at \$4,200 per month, or **\$50,400 per year**, based on an informal Q1 2022 quote. There is **no written agreement**, and the lease does not mention the service. Operations believes the arrangement began about when Pinnacle moved in (early 2022). The workbook itself describes the service as provided “at no charge per informal arrangement” and the value as “unreimbursed.” The Compliance Manual lists “[f]ree courier services, specimen pick-up, or delivery services” as remuneration and prohibits in-kind benefits without a written FMV agreement (§ 4.2).')
H('Analysis', 3)
P('The legal character of the service turns on **what the courier carries and for whom**.')
B('A laboratory that collects specimens it will itself test, solely to perform its own service, is generally not viewed as conferring independent value on the referring physician. The Stark definition of remuneration also excludes items, devices and supplies used solely to collect, transport, process or store specimens for the entity furnishing them (§ 411.351).')
B('That exclusion covers **items**, not services. Government guidance has long treated courier services that do more than transport the lab’s own specimens as suspect: carrying specimens to other labs, moving specimens or records between the physician’s offices, delivering supplies, or relieving the practice of its own transport costs.')
P('Greenfield runs in-house laboratories at 8 sites. Daily pickups at all 12 sites therefore raise a real question whether Pinnacle’s couriers also move Greenfield’s own specimens (for example, from satellite sites without labs to Greenfield’s in-house labs), records or supplies. If they do, the service is remuneration from a DHS entity to Greenfield. No exception applies to an unwritten, no-charge service arrangement, so each owner’s Pinnacle referrals would be prohibited. This would be independent of the lease defect, and the AKS problem would be stronger still. Greenfield’s own description of the value as “unreimbursed” is unhelpful.')
H('Remediation', 3)
N('Under privilege, interview Operations and site managers and obtain Pinnacle route manifests to establish the scope of the courier service. Determine whether any non-Pinnacle specimens, inter-office transfers, records or supplies were carried.')
N('If the service is limited to Pinnacle-tested specimens, document that in a written protocol signed by both parties. If it is broader, either end the non-Pinnacle uses or have Greenfield pay FMV under a signed services agreement.')
N('Quantify any non-exempt value (about \$4,200 per month is the internal estimate) for the disclosure analysis. Treat Issues 3 and 4 together as the “Pinnacle relationship.”')

H('Issue 5 — Buckeye Surgical Center: Referral-Based Distributions and the Greenfield “Referral Credit” (Critical under AKS; Medium under Stark)', 2)
H('Facts', 3)
B('**Buckeye level.** The Buckeye OA allocates net profits and losses “exclusively” by each member’s **Referral Percentage**, “not … in proportion to Membership Interests” (§ 4.1(a)–(b)). It distributes cash quarterly the same way (§ 4.2), as well as released reserves (§ 4.4). Referral Percentage is each member’s share of surgical cases referred to the Center. For Greenfield, that means cases referred by its physicians (§§ 1.9, 1.25–1.26).')
B('**Monitoring.** Greenfield, as Manager, tracks referrals, and members must report referral data (§§ 4.2(b), 6.2).')
B('**Utilization.** Physician members must “use commercially reasonable efforts … to utilize the Center” (§ 6.1). This sits awkwardly beside § 5.5(b), which disclaims any referral requirement “provided, however, that distributions … shall be allocated based on Referral Percentage.”')
B('**Greenfield’s representation.** In the Buckeye OA, Greenfield represented that it would pass Buckeye distributions to referring physicians through a “referral credit” (§ 4.5).')
B('**Greenfield level.** Under the Greenfield OA, Greenfield’s Buckeye returns are allocated first as **Referral Credits** equal to **0.5% of the facility fee revenue of each case a member refers to Buckeye**. Only the remainder is distributed pro rata (§ 8.4(b)). The credit is said to “align Member incentives with the success of the Company’s affiliated surgical center.”')
B('**2023 Referral Credits:** \$36,900 on 900 cases at an average \$8,200 facility fee. Dr. Stein received \$14,022 on 342 cases.')
B('**Employed physicians.** Separately, they earn \$150 RQB payments for Buckeye referrals (Issue 1).')
B('**Medical directorship.** Dr. Stein, a 25% personal owner, is also Buckeye’s paid Medical Director (Issue 6).')
B('**Contradictory internal statements.** The January 2022 Compensation Plan memo tells physicians that member profit distributions are “ownership-proportional and are not allocated on the basis of referral activity” (§ 6). The 2023 compensation notes repeat that statement (citing OA § 8.1). Both are contradicted by OA § 8.4 and by the Referral Credit column in the same workbook.')
H('Analysis', 3)
P('**Stark.** The relator alleges that the surgical procedures are DHS (Compl. ¶¶ 73, 87). That is wrong as a general matter. ASC facility services paid under the ASC payment system are excluded from the DHS definition (§ 411.351), so ownership of Buckeye is not, by itself, an ownership interest in a DHS entity. Count III’s Stark theory is therefore weak, and its “group practice” citation to § 411.352(i) concerns profit shares from the group’s DHS, not ASC returns. The Stark spillover risks are narrower:')
B('if Buckeye bills any items or services outside the ASC composite rate that are DHS (e.g., certain separately paid drugs, prosthetics or DME), referral-based distributions would implicate Stark directly;')
B('member compensation from Greenfield that turns on referrals to an affiliate gives the government a § 411.352(g) argument, because Referral Credits are part of member “compensation” from the group. It is also poor optics for any claim that Greenfield’s compensation design is referral-neutral.')
P('These points must be confirmed with Buckeye’s claims data.')
P('**AKS (the principal exposure).** Returns on investment tied to the investor’s referrals are a central concern of the AKS. The ASC safe harbor (§ 1001.952(r)) requires, among other things, that returns be **directly proportional to capital invested**. It also contains investor-qualification, “one-third” income and practice tests, and requires that investors not be required or encouraged to refer. The Buckeye OA does the opposite in express terms: it makes referrals the *exclusive* measure of return and imposes a utilization covenant. Greenfield’s 0.5%-per-case credit converts each referral into a traceable personal payment, with the CFO tracking cases and reporting them quarterly (OA § 8.4(c)). These provisions have been in place since 2016 (Buckeye) and since at least 2020 (Greenfield). Buckeye’s Medicare and Medicaid facility claims for patients referred by Greenfield physicians are at risk as AKS-tainted FCA claims. The relator alleges about \$16.8 million in Medicare and Medicaid revenue for Buckeye in 2023 (Compl. ¶ 11). Ohio fee-splitting and related professional-conduct provisions (Ohio Rev. Code Chapter 4731) should also be reviewed.')
P('**Ownership records do not reconcile.** The Buckeye OA (never amended; transfers need the consent of all members, § 8.1) shows only three members: Greenfield 60%, Stein 25%, Narayan 15%. The 2023 compensation summary instead reports Buckeye ownership percentages for some 30 other Greenfield members, e.g., Adler 5.0%, Castillo 4.5%, Banerjee 4.0%. With Stein’s 25% and Narayan’s 15%, individual percentages total **113.5%**. Possible explanations:')
B('look-through attributions of Greenfield’s 60%, although those would not total 73.5%;')
B('undocumented transfers;')
B('data errors.')
P('Each has different AKS consequences, and the figures must be reconciled. The 900 credited cases are attributed entirely to 14 member physicians, while the relator alleges 702 Greenfield-referred cases (78%). The Buckeye OA’s “hypothetical” illustration uses exactly 702/342/56, and 342 is Dr. Stein’s actual 2023 count. This tends to undercut the label “hypothetical” and will be used to show that the drafters modeled actual referrals.')
H('Remediation', 3)
N('**Immediately suspend** Referral Credit allocations (OA § 8.4(b)). Hold Greenfield’s Buckeye returns in a segregated account pending counsel’s advice.')
N('Amend the **Buckeye OA** (all-member written consent, § 12.2(b)) so that allocations and distributions are strictly pro rata to capital and Membership Interests. Delete §§ 1.9, 1.25, 1.26, 4.5 and 6.2 and the utilization covenant in § 6.1. Restructure toward the ASC safe harbor, recognizing that a hospital-free, multispecialty, group-practice-investor ASC must meet the specific investor and income tests in § 1001.952(r).')
N('Amend the **Greenfield OA** (two-thirds vote) to delete § 8.4(b) and the Referral Credit definition, and to distribute Buckeye returns by Membership Interest. Correct the inaccurate statements in the 2022 Compensation memo.')
N('Reconcile Buckeye’s capitalization and ownership history. Obtain capital-contribution records (redacted in Ex. A) and all distribution statements since 2016. Determine whether any DHS is billed by Buckeye.')
N('Evaluate an **OIG Self-Disclosure Protocol** submission for the Buckeye conduct, coordinated with the overall strategy (Part VII). The CMS SRDP covers only Stark and is not the right vehicle for AKS conduct.')
N('Advise Dr. Stein and Dr. Narayan to retain **separate counsel**. They are named defendants and personally received referral-based Buckeye distributions.')

B('**Medical directorship.** Dr. Stein, a 25% personal owner, is also Buckeye\u2019s paid Medical Director (Issue 6).')
B('**Contradictory internal statements.** The January 2022 Compensation Plan memo tells physicians that member profit distributions are \u201cownership-proportional and are not allocated on the basis of referral activity\u201d (\u00a7 6). The 2023 compensation notes repeat that statement (citing OA \u00a7 8.1). Both are contradicted by OA \u00a7 8.4 and by the Referral Credit column in the same workbook.')
H('Analysis', 3)
P('**Stark.** The relator alleges that the surgical procedures are DHS (Compl. \u00b6\u00b6 73, 87). That is wrong as a general matter. ASC facility services paid under the ASC payment system are excluded from the DHS definition (\u00a7 411.351), so ownership of Buckeye is not, by itself, an ownership interest in a DHS entity. Count III\u2019s Stark theory is therefore weak, and its \u201cgroup practice\u201d citation to \u00a7 411.352(i) concerns profit shares from the group\u2019s DHS, not ASC returns. The Stark spillover risks are narrower:')
B('if Buckeye bills any items or services outside the ASC composite rate that are DHS (e.g., certain separately paid drugs, prosthetics or DME), referral-based distributions would implicate Stark directly;')
B('member compensation from Greenfield that turns on referrals to an affiliate gives the government a \u00a7 411.352(g) argument, because Referral Credits are part of member \u201ccompensation\u201d from the group. It is also poor optics for any claim that Greenfield\u2019s compensation design is referral-neutral.')
P('These points must be confirmed with Buckeye\u2019s claims data.')
P('**AKS (the principal exposure).** Returns on investment tied to the investor\u2019s referrals are a central concern of the AKS. The ASC safe harbor (\u00a7 1001.952(r)) requires, among other things, that returns be **directly proportional to capital invested**. It also contains investor-qualification, \u201cone-third\u201d income and practice tests, and requires that investors not be required or encouraged to refer. The Buckeye OA does the opposite in express terms: it makes referrals the *exclusive* measure of return and imposes a utilization covenant. Greenfield\u2019s 0.5%-per-case credit converts each referral into a traceable personal payment, with the CFO tracking cases and reporting them quarterly (OA \u00a7 8.4(c)). These provisions have been in place since 2016 (Buckeye) and since at least 2020 (Greenfield). Buckeye\u2019s Medicare and Medicaid facility claims for patients referred by Greenfield physicians are at risk as AKS-tainted FCA claims. The relator alleges about \$16.8 million in Medicare and Medicaid revenue for Buckeye in 2023 (Compl. \u00b6 11). Ohio fee-splitting and related professional-conduct provisions (Ohio Rev. Code Chapter 4731) should also be reviewed.')
P('**Ownership records do not reconcile.** The Buckeye OA (never amended; transfers need the consent of all members, \u00a7 8.1) shows only three members: Greenfield 60%, Stein 25%, Narayan 15%. The 2023 compensation summary instead reports Buckeye ownership percentages for some 30 other Greenfield members, e.g., Adler 5.0%, Castillo 4.5%, Banerjee 4.0%. With Stein\u2019s 25% and Narayan\u2019s 15%, individual percentages total **113.5%**. Possible explanations:')
B('look-through attributions of Greenfield\u2019s 60%, although those would not total 73.5%;')
B('undocumented transfers;')
B('data errors.')
P('Each has different AKS consequences, and the figures must be reconciled. The 900 credited cases are attributed entirely to 14 member physicians, while the relator alleges 702 Greenfield-referred cases (78%). The Buckeye OA\u2019s \u201chypothetical\u201d illustration uses exactly 702/342/56, and 342 is Dr. Stein\u2019s actual 2023 count. This tends to undercut the label \u201chypothetical\u201d and will be used to show that the drafters modeled actual referrals.')
H('Remediation', 3)
N('**Immediately suspend** Referral Credit allocations (OA \u00a7 8.4(b)). Hold Greenfield\u2019s Buckeye returns in a segregated account pending counsel\u2019s advice.')
N('Amend the **Buckeye OA** (all-member written consent, \u00a7 12.2(b)) so that allocations and distributions are strictly pro rata to capital and Membership Interests. Delete \u00a7\u00a7 1.9, 1.25, 1.26, 4.5 and 6.2 and the utilization covenant in \u00a7 6.1. Restructure toward the ASC safe harbor, recognizing that a hospital-free, multispecialty, group-practice-investor ASC must meet the specific investor and income tests in \u00a7 1001.952(r).')
N('Amend the **Greenfield OA** (two-thirds vote) to delete \u00a7 8.4(b) and the Referral Credit definition, and to distribute Buckeye returns by Membership Interest. Correct the inaccurate statements in the 2022 Compensation memo.')
N('Reconcile Buckeye\u2019s capitalization and ownership history. Obtain capital-contribution records (redacted in Ex. A) and all distribution statements since 2016. Determine whether any DHS is billed by Buckeye.')
N('Evaluate an **OIG Self-Disclosure Protocol** submission for the Buckeye conduct, coordinated with the overall strategy (Part VII). The CMS SRDP covers only Stark and is not the right vehicle for AKS conduct.')
N('Advise Dr. Stein and Dr. Narayan to retain **separate counsel**. They are named defendants and personally received referral-based Buckeye distributions.')

H('Issue 6 — Dr. Stein’s Buckeye Medical Director Agreement (High)', 2)
H('Facts', 3)
B('**Terms.** The agreement is dated August 22, 2016, the same day Buckeye was formed. It pays **\$120,000 per year** (\$10,000 per month) for a **minimum of 8 hours per month (96 hours per year)** (§§ 3.2, 4.1). That is **\$1,250 per contracted hour**.')
B('**Itemized duties.** Exhibit A itemizes only about **40 hours per year**: 8 for meetings, 24 for monthly metrics review and 8 for policy review. The rest is “as needed.” Measured against itemized hours alone, the rate is \$3,000 per hour.')
B('**Renewal.** The agreement renews automatically each year “on the same terms … as of the Effective Date” with “[n]o additional action, approval, or documentation” (§§ 2.2–2.3). The Buckeye OA bars any change without the Medical Director’s consent (§ 5.4(d)).')
B('**Time records.** Dr. Stein must keep contemporaneous time records (§ 3.2). None are in the file.')
B('**Approvals.** Dr. Narayan, a 15% co-owner and Dr. Stein’s fellow Compensation Committee member, signed for Buckeye. Greenfield’s OA says the agreement “was approved by the Compensation Committee” (§ 10.1), which Dr. Stein chairs. The file copy shows blank signature lines for both parties.')
B('**FMV support.** We found no FMV opinion for the medical directorship. The 2019 Lakeshore study covered physician compensation, not this arrangement. The \$120,000 has been paid unchanged for over eight years, about \$960,000 through August 2024.')
B('**Complaint.** The relator alleges “over \$200,000 annually” (Compl. ¶ 12). The documents show \$120,000.')
H('Analysis', 3)
P('**Stark.** Because Buckeye is an ASC rather than a DHS entity, the agreement is not itself a Stark compensation arrangement with a DHS entity. An indirect compensation arrangement with Greenfield, which owns 60% of Buckeye, would require Dr. Stein’s aggregate compensation from Buckeye to vary with or take into account his referrals to Greenfield (§ 411.354(c)(2)). A flat fee generally does not. Stark risk is therefore secondary, but that conclusion depends on the fee being fixed and on there being no side payments.')
P('**AKS.** This is the principal exposure. The personal services safe harbor (§ 1001.952(d)) requires that compensation be consistent with FMV and not determined by referrals. The agreement presents a high-risk profile:')
B('an hourly-equivalent rate that appears well above typical administrative medical director benchmarks;')
B('duties that substantially overlap with those of an owner and ASC governing-body leader;')
B('no documented time;')
B('no re-benchmarking in eight years;')
B('approval by conflicted insiders;')
B('a recipient who is the ASC’s largest individual referral source (342 of 900 cases in 2023).')
P('Together these support an inference that the fee is a disguised return to a referral source. The fee also adds to Dr. Stein’s total compensation of about \$1,358,022 in 2023. The relator’s figure of \$1,224,000 omits the directorship fee and the Referral Credits.')
H('Remediation', 3)
N('Obtain Dr. Stein’s time logs for 2016 to the present, and Medical Advisory Committee minutes, credentialing files and quality reports, to substantiate the services.')
N('Commission an independent FMV and commercial-reasonableness opinion on the directorship, based on the hours actually needed and documented.')
N('Restate the agreement with: hourly or capped compensation at FMV; mandatory monthly time sheets as a condition of payment; a defined duty list; a fixed term with renewal only on documented FMV review; and approval by unconflicted Buckeye members, or an independent manager if none are available. Remove the consent lock in Buckeye OA § 5.4(d).')
N('Evaluate whether payments exceeding documented FMV must be repaid as part of the disclosure strategy.')

H('Issue 7 — IOASE “Same Building” and Supervision Gaps at Hilliard (Loc. 7) and Dublin (Loc. 9) (High)', 2)
H('Facts', 3)
B('**Testing.** Laboratory and point-of-care testing (blood draws, urinalysis, glucose and lipid panels) runs **daily**, performed by medical assistants and lab technicians.')
B('**Physician presence.** A physician is on site about **2 days per week at Hilliard** and **3 half-days per week at Dublin**. The designated supervising physicians were at the main campus, 14 and 17 miles away, during the March 2022 site visits. Staff reported that “we call if we have questions” (audit memo § III.A).')
B('**Internal policy.** Manual § 5.2 requires direct, on-site supervision for all DHS. It forbids furnishing DHS when a supervising physician is absent and requires supervision logs.')
B('**Follow-up.** The audit recommended corrective action in March 2022. The file contains no evidence of remediation, supervision logs, or quantification of affected volume.')
H('Analysis', 3)
P('**Supervision.** The IOASE requires that DHS be furnished by the referring physician, by a group member, or by individuals supervised “in accordance with” applicable Medicare payment and coverage rules (§ 411.355(b)(1)). For most clinical laboratory tests, Medicare’s physician-supervision levels for diagnostic tests do not apply in the way they do to imaging; laboratory oversight is governed by CLIA. Remote laboratory oversight may therefore not, by itself, defeat the IOASE. It would, however, breach Greenfield’s own stricter policy, which matters for scienter and credibility. Counsel should confirm:')
B('that each site holds a CLIA certificate (or waiver) appropriate to the tests performed;')
B('that the CLIA laboratory director requirements are met;')
B('that no imaging or other non-laboratory DHS at these sites requires direct supervision.')
P('**“Same building” test (the more serious IOASE risk).** Each referral must meet one of three alternatives in § 411.355(b)(2)(i):')
B('(A) the office is open at least 35 hours per week **and** the referring physician or group members regularly practice there at least 30 hours per week, part of it furnishing non-DHS physician services;')
B('(B) the office is open at least 8 hours per week **and** the *referring* physician regularly practices there at least 6 hours per week;')
B('(C) the office is open at least 8 hours per week **and** the referring physician or a group member is present and orders the DHS during a patient visit, or is present while the DHS is furnished.')
P('With roughly 16 physician hours per week at Hilliard and about 12 at Dublin, test (A) appears unmet. Test (B) protects only referrals by physicians who regularly practice at the site. Test (C) fails on days when no physician is present. Specimens collected on physician-absent days, or ordered by physicians who do not regularly practice at the site (for example, orders from the main campus or orders by non-physician practitioners acting for absent physicians), are likely outside the IOASE. The “centralized building” alternative requires full-time exclusive use by the group and is unlikely to apply to these offices.')
H('Remediation', 3)
N('Immediately limit testing at Hilliard and Dublin to sessions when an ordering physician or group member is present, or to physicians who meet test (B). Alternatively, route specimens to a centralized building or to the main-campus laboratory.')
N('Implement the supervision logs Manual § 5.2 requires. Audit them quarterly.')
N('Quantify Medicare and Medicaid laboratory DHS at both sites since 2019 by date, ordering physician and physician presence. Include the results in the overpayment analysis. Note that all post-2022 DHS is already exposed under Issue 2, so this analysis matters most for the pre-RQB period and for any period after the RQB ends.')
N('Survey the other six laboratory sites for the same pattern.')

H('Issue 8 — Independent-Contractor Radiologists Billed Under the Group NPI (Medium)', 2)
H('Facts', 3)
P('Four 1099 radiologists (Drs. Okafor, Tanaka, Brooks and Rivas; \$290,000–\$310,000 each in 2023) read about **30% of Greenfield’s imaging studies**. They furnish about **60%** of their professional services through Greenfield and the rest through other facilities and teleradiology. All of their professional interpretations are billed under Greenfield’s group NPI and TIN. The 2022 audit concluded that they fail the 75% “substantially all” test, which would defeat the IOASE for their reads. It recommended conversion to employment or membership, or billing under individual NPIs. Hotline #2023-11 (Aug. 2023) raised the same concern. It was closed with “no further action” because the radiologists “provide services per contract,” without Committee or counsel review.')
H('Analysis', 3)
P('The audit memo and Manual §§ 3.2.5 and 5.4 **misstate the law**, and the misstatement cuts both ways.')
B('**The test is an aggregate measure of members only.** The “substantially all” test in § 411.352(d) asks whether at least 75% of the total patient care services of all group *members* (owners and employees) are furnished through the group. It is not a per-physician threshold, and IC physicians are not “members of the group” (§ 411.351). The four ICs’ 60% share therefore does not by itself defeat group-practice status. On the audit’s data (52 members assumed at the threshold; 31 of 35 employees at or above 75%; 4 employees at about 50%), the aggregate test appears satisfied, subject to verification.')
B('**The real risks lie elsewhere.**')
B('(i) **IOASE furnishing element.** ICs may be “physicians in the group practice” only for the time they furnish services to group patients in the group’s facilities under a contractual arrangement (§ 411.351). Whether a professional component personally performed by a non-member IC, particularly one read remotely, fits § 411.355(b)(1) and the location requirements requires analysis. Off-site teleradiology reads are the most exposed.', 1)
B('(ii) **Anti-markup rule.** For diagnostic tests billed by a supplier that did not perform them, payment is limited unless the performing physician “shares a practice” with the billing supplier. That requires furnishing substantially all (75%) of professional services through the billing group, or meeting the site-of-service test (42 C.F.R. § 414.50). At 60%, the ICs likely fail the substantially-all prong, so the site-of-service analysis is critical. Overbilling under the anti-markup rule is an overpayment independent of Stark.', 1)
B('(iii) **Reassignment.** Each IC’s reassignment of benefits must be valid (CMS-855R; 42 C.F.R. § 424.80), with joint and several liability language and records access.', 1)
H('Remediation', 3)
N('Obtain the four IC agreements, CMS-855R reassignments, read-location logs and billing data. Determine where each professional component was performed.')
N('Prospectively, either employ the radiologists, or bill their off-site reads in compliance with the anti-markup rule, or have them bill directly.')
N('Correct Manual §§ 3.2.5 and 5.4 and train billing staff on the correct tests.')
N('Quantify any anti-markup or IOASE overpayment for the disclosure analysis.')

H('Issue 9 — ClearView Diagnostic Imaging Lease: FMV Likely Defensible, but Undocumented and Expired (Medium)', 2)
H('Facts', 3)
B('**Lease terms.** Suite 210, 3,200 sf, January 1, 2021 to December 31, 2025. One 3-year renewal option at a “mutually agreed” rate; 150% month-to-month holdover rent.')
B('**Rent structure.** Base rent of **\$18.00/sf (\$57,600/yr)**, fixed, with no concessions (§§ 4.1, 4.3, 4.6). **In addition**, the tenant pays its pro rata share (6.67%) of **all** building operating expenses: taxes, insurance, CAM, utilities, management and repairs (§§ 4.5, 5.1–5.3). Year-1 operating expenses were estimated at **\$12.00/sf**, or **\$38,419/yr** (Ex. B).')
B('**Tenant improvements.** The tenant paid 100% of its specialized build-out (lead shielding, electrical, supplemental HVAC) with no landlord contribution (§ 7.1).')
B('**Comparisons made by others.** The 2022 audit, hotline #2023-14 and the complaint (¶¶ 55–56) all compared the \$18 base rent directly with the \$28–\$32/sf **full-service-gross** appraisal range. The complaint alleges a subsidy of \$32,000–\$44,800 per year and “over \$250,000” over the term. Arithmetically, the maximum is \$224,000 (5 × \$44,800).')
B('**Referral dependence.** About 68% of ClearView’s patients are said to come from Greenfield (Compl. ¶ 58). ClearView represents that no physician or physician group has an ownership or financial interest in it (§ 15.3).')
B('**Management’s explanation.** Management attributed the rate to “tenant improvement credits” (audit memo § IV). The lease contains no TI credit.')
H('Analysis', 3)
P('Stated on a gross-equivalent basis, ClearView’s rent is about **\$30.00/sf** (\$18.00 base plus about \$12.00 in expense pass-throughs). Annual occupancy cost is about \$96,000, inside the appraisal’s Suite 210 range of \$89,600–\$102,400. The lease was signed about four months after the appraisal’s value date, inside the 12-month window the appraiser specified. The appraisal also assumed landlord-delivered standard TI, while ClearView bore all of its build-out. If expenses were in fact billed and collected at or near the estimate, the lease is **likely defensible on FMV** under § 411.357(a), and the complaint’s Count II theory as to ClearView is materially overstated. Greenfield should rely on this gross-equivalent analysis and not on the unsupported “TI credit” explanation, which the lease contradicts.')
P('Residual risks:')
B('**Collection.** Whether the annual reconciliations under § 5.3 were actually issued and collected. If they were not, effective rent was \$18/sf and the lease is below FMV.')
B('**Exclusive use and execution.** Whether the exclusive-use requirement was honored, and whether a fully executed copy exists. The file copy has blank signatures and the floor-plan exhibit was “to be attached.”')
B('**Ownership representation.** Whether the § 15.3 no-physician-ownership representation is true. Any ownership by a Greenfield physician would create a Stark ownership interest that no exception covers.')
B('**Status after expiration.** The lease expired December 31, 2025. Any renewal at a “mutually agreed” rate must be written, FMV-supported by a *current* appraisal, and approved by unconflicted decision-makers. Holdover at 150% is permissible under § 411.357(a)(7) only if the arrangement otherwise met the exception.')
H('Remediation', 3)
N('Pull the 2021–2025 operating-expense estimates, reconciliations and payment history, and a fully executed copy. Prepare a privileged FMV memorandum documenting the gross-equivalent analysis.')
N('Determine the current status (renewal, holdover or vacancy). Obtain a current appraisal and paper any renewal at FMV.')
N('Obtain an ownership certification from ClearView. Re-open hotline #2023-14 under counsel and document the corrected analysis.')
N('Retrieve and review the **Ohio Heart & Vascular Associates** lease (Suite 310; terms “on file” but not produced). At \$30/sf it appears within range, but the lease basis (gross or net) and term are unknown. If OHVA physicians refer DHS to Greenfield, the lease must meet § 411.357(a) with Greenfield as the DHS entity.')
EOF

B('**The test is an aggregate measure of members only.** The \u201csubstantially all\u201d test in \u00a7 411.352(d) asks whether at least 75% of the total patient care services of all group *members* (owners and employees) are furnished through the group. It is not a per-physician threshold, and IC physicians are not \u201cmembers of the group\u201d (\u00a7 411.351). The four ICs\u2019 60% share therefore does not by itself defeat group-practice status. On the audit\u2019s data (52 members assumed at the threshold; 31 of 35 employees at or above 75%; 4 employees at about 50%), the aggregate test appears satisfied, subject to verification.')
B('**The real risks lie elsewhere.**')
B('(i) **IOASE furnishing element.** ICs may be \u201cphysicians in the group practice\u201d only for the time they furnish services to group patients in the group\u2019s facilities under a contractual arrangement (\u00a7 411.351). Whether a professional component personally performed by a non-member IC, particularly one read remotely, fits \u00a7 411.355(b)(1) and the location requirements requires analysis. Off-site teleradiology reads are the most exposed.', 1)
B('(ii) **Anti-markup rule.** For diagnostic tests billed by a supplier that did not perform them, payment is limited unless the performing physician \u201cshares a practice\u201d with the billing supplier. That requires furnishing substantially all (75%) of professional services through the billing group, or meeting the site-of-service test (42 C.F.R. \u00a7 414.50). At 60%, the ICs likely fail the substantially-all prong, so the site-of-service analysis is critical. Overbilling under the anti-markup rule is an overpayment independent of Stark.', 1)
B('(iii) **Reassignment.** Each IC\u2019s reassignment of benefits must be valid (CMS-855R; 42 C.F.R. \u00a7 424.80), with joint and several liability language and records access.', 1)
H('Remediation', 3)
N('Obtain the four IC agreements, CMS-855R reassignments, read-location logs and billing data. Determine where each professional component was performed.')
N('Prospectively, either employ the radiologists, or bill their off-site reads in compliance with the anti-markup rule, or have them bill directly.')
N('Correct Manual \u00a7\u00a7 3.2.5 and 5.4 and train billing staff on the correct tests.')
N('Quantify any anti-markup or IOASE overpayment for the disclosure analysis.')

H('Issue 9 \u2014 ClearView Diagnostic Imaging Lease: FMV Likely Defensible, but Undocumented and Expired (Medium)', 2)
H('Facts', 3)
B('**Lease terms.** Suite 210, 3,200 sf, January 1, 2021 to December 31, 2025. One 3-year renewal option at a \u201cmutually agreed\u201d rate; 150% month-to-month holdover rent.')
B('**Rent structure.** Base rent of **\$18.00/sf (\$57,600/yr)**, fixed, with no concessions (\u00a7\u00a7 4.1, 4.3, 4.6). **In addition**, the tenant pays its pro rata share (6.67%) of **all** building operating expenses: taxes, insurance, CAM, utilities, management and repairs (\u00a7\u00a7 4.5, 5.1\u20135.3). Year-1 operating expenses were estimated at **\$12.00/sf**, or **\$38,419/yr** (Ex. B).')
B('**Tenant improvements.** The tenant paid 100% of its specialized build-out (lead shielding, electrical, supplemental HVAC) with no landlord contribution (\u00a7 7.1).')
B('**Comparisons made by others.** The 2022 audit, hotline #2023-14 and the complaint (\u00b6\u00b6 55\u201356) all compared the \$18 base rent directly with the \$28\u2013\$32/sf **full-service-gross** appraisal range. The complaint alleges a subsidy of \$32,000\u2013\$44,800 per year and \u201cover \$250,000\u201d over the term. Arithmetically, the maximum is \$224,000 (5 \u00d7 \$44,800).')
B('**Referral dependence.** About 68% of ClearView\u2019s patients are said to come from Greenfield (Compl. \u00b6 58). ClearView represents that no physician or physician group has an ownership or financial interest in it (\u00a7 15.3).')
B('**Management\u2019s explanation.** Management attributed the rate to \u201ctenant improvement credits\u201d (audit memo \u00a7 IV). The lease contains no TI credit.')
H('Analysis', 3)
P('Stated on a gross-equivalent basis, ClearView\u2019s rent is about **\$30.00/sf** (\$18.00 base plus about \$12.00 in expense pass-throughs). Annual occupancy cost is about \$96,000, inside the appraisal\u2019s Suite 210 range of \$89,600\u2013\$102,400. The lease was signed about four months after the appraisal\u2019s value date, inside the 12-month window the appraiser specified. The appraisal also assumed landlord-delivered standard TI, while ClearView bore all of its build-out. If expenses were in fact billed and collected at or near the estimate, the lease is **likely defensible on FMV** under \u00a7 411.357(a), and the complaint\u2019s Count II theory as to ClearView is materially overstated. Greenfield should rely on this gross-equivalent analysis and not on the unsupported \u201cTI credit\u201d explanation, which the lease contradicts.')
P('Residual risks:')
B('**Collection.** Whether the annual reconciliations under \u00a7 5.3 were actually issued and collected. If they were not, effective rent was \$18/sf and the lease is below FMV.')
B('**Exclusive use and execution.** Whether the exclusive-use requirement was honored, and whether a fully executed copy exists. The file copy has blank signatures and the floor-plan exhibit was \u201cto be attached.\u201d')
B('**Ownership representation.** Whether the \u00a7 15.3 no-physician-ownership representation is true. Any ownership by a Greenfield physician would create a Stark ownership interest that no exception covers.')
B('**Status after expiration.** The lease expired December 31, 2025. Any renewal at a \u201cmutually agreed\u201d rate must be written, FMV-supported by a *current* appraisal, and approved by unconflicted decision-makers. Holdover at 150% is permissible under \u00a7 411.357(a)(7) only if the arrangement otherwise met the exception.')
H('Remediation', 3)
N('Pull the 2021\u20132025 operating-expense estimates, reconciliations and payment history, and a fully executed copy. Prepare a privileged FMV memorandum documenting the gross-equivalent analysis.')
N('Determine the current status (renewal, holdover or vacancy). Obtain a current appraisal and paper any renewal at FMV.')
N('Obtain an ownership certification from ClearView. Re-open hotline #2023-14 under counsel and document the corrected analysis.')
N('Retrieve and review the **Ohio Heart & Vascular Associates** lease (Suite 310; terms \u201con file\u201d but not produced). At \$30/sf it appears within range, but the lease basis (gross or net) and term are unknown. If OHVA physicians refer DHS to Greenfield, the lease must meet \u00a7 411.357(a) with Greenfield as the DHS entity.')
EOF

H('Issue 10 — Physician Compensation Governance, FMV Support and Self-Dealing (Medium)', 2)
H('Facts', 3)
B('**Committee composition.** The Compensation Committee is Dr. Stein (chair), Dr. Narayan and the CFO. It sets **member** base salaries (60th percentile MGMA) and quality bonuses, including its own members’ pay. Its decisions require only its own majority vote, with “no additional approval requirements” (OA § 7.3(b)). There is no charter: Exhibit B was confirmed missing by the CCO in October 2024. Employed physicians’ base salaries are set by Dr. Stein with CFO approval (OA § 7.5(a)).')
B('**Stale benchmarks.** The only benchmarking study is Lakeshore’s November 2019 study of 2018–2019 data. In December 2021 the Committee “confirmed [its] continued appropriateness” without new data (Comp. Memo §§ 1–2). As of February 2024 no update had been commissioned (Comp. Summary, Notes). In September 2024 the CFO called the study “pretty dated,” and the item was deferred.')
B('**Quality bonuses above the cap.** Quality bonuses are capped at 25% of base salary (OA § 7.2(b)). In 2023 they were paid at or within the cap for every member **except the two physician members of the Compensation Committee**:')
B('Dr. Stein: \$215,000 on an \$847,000 base (25.4%; \$3,250 over the cap);', 1)
B('Dr. Narayan: \$188,000 on a \$612,000 base (30.7%; **\$35,000 over the cap**).', 1)
B('**Profit distributions not pro rata.** Profit distributions should follow ownership (OA § 8.2). For nearly all members they work out to about \$38,100–\$38,200 per 1% of ownership. Dr. Stein received \$162,000, about \$1,800 above pro rata for 4.2%. Dr. Narayan received \$97,000, about \$21,000 below pro rata for 3.1%. Neither variance is explained.')
B('**Inconsistent quality-bonus weightings.** The OA weights patient satisfaction 40%, clinical quality 40% and documentation 20% (§ 7.2(b)). The 2022 memo describes 50/50 patient satisfaction and clinical quality and omits documentation (§ 6).')
B('**Totals.** Dr. Stein’s 2023 total from Greenfield and Buckeye-related sources was \$1,358,022. That excludes his personal 25% Buckeye distributions, which are not in the file.')
H('Analysis', 3)
P('The group-practice rules do not require member compensation to be at FMV. What matters for Stark is that compensation not vary with DHS referrals (§ 411.352(g)) and that profit shares and productivity bonuses follow a documented method (§ 411.352(i), including (i)(4)). Payments that depart from the OA’s own formulas, with no documented basis, weaken Greenfield’s ability to show that its compensation follows the stated, referral-neutral methods. Under the AKS, above-formula payments to the two most significant referral sources and decision-makers, approved by themselves, are a classic red flag. FMV for employed physicians is a direct element of § 411.357(c). Reliance on 2018–2019 data for 2022–2024 compensation, with no contemporaneous FMV analysis of total compensation (base, productivity and RQB), leaves the FMV element unsupported. That gap is separate from the RQB problem.')
H('Remediation', 3)
N('Reconstitute the Compensation Committee with independent members, or at least non-conflicted members. Adopt a written charter with mandatory recusal for any matter affecting a member’s own compensation or an affiliate in which the member has an interest.')
N('Engage an independent valuation firm to benchmark all physician compensation (2022–present and prospectively), including commercial reasonableness for the highest-paid physicians and the medical directorship.')
N('Reconcile and document the 2023 quality-bonus and profit-distribution variances. Recover or re-characterize overpayments according to the OA, after counsel’s review.')
N('Conform the OA, the Compensation Plan and the employment agreements to one consistent set of documented formulas.')

H('Issue 11 — Compliance Program Breakdown and Mishandling of Stark Reports (High)', 2)
H('Facts', 3)
B('**Conflicted oversight.** The Compliance Committee is chaired by Dr. Stein, the architect and principal beneficiary of the arrangements at issue. Its other members are Dr. Narayan (Buckeye co-owner, Compensation Committee member) and the CFO (co-author of the RQB, lease negotiator). The CCO is formally to report to the Committee (Manual § 2.2; OA § 6.3(b)), but OA § 6.1(d) gives the Managing Member “supervision and direction” of the CCO. The relator alleges the CCO reports to the CFO (Compl. ¶ 95).')
B('**Meetings.** The Committee did not meet in Q4 2023. The Q3 2024 meeting was pushed to December, leaving about six months without a meeting, because Dr. Stein was “slammed with cases at Buckeye.” The Manual requires quarterly meetings (Manual § 2.1; OA § 7.4).')
B('**Training.** Annual training is required by Q1 each year (Manual § 7.1). It was not held in 2023 or 2024. The 2022 audit, the 2023 hotline log and the 2024 e-mail are inconsistent on whether training occurred in 2022.')
B('**Risk assessments.** Annual risk assessments are required (Manual § 8.1). None has been done since the March 2022 audit; the September 2024 e-mail says none since April 2021. The Manual has not had its required annual review (§ 12).')
B('**Stark-related hotline reports.** Three 2023 reports were Stark-related: #2023-07 (RQB), #2023-11 (IC radiologists) and #2023-14 (ClearView rent). Each was closed “Resolved — No Action” with “N/A” committee review and no counsel. That contravenes Manual § 6.3 (Committee notice within 5 business days; Committee review of findings) and § 2.3 (outside counsel for potential Stark/AKS violations). The investigations consisted of confirming that the arrangements matched their own documents.')
B('**The 2022 audit.** The March 2022 audit, labeled “privileged” but not conducted by or at the direction of counsel (§ II, “No outside counsel was engaged”), identified the satellite, radiologist and lease issues. It found “no compliance concerns” with the RQB, made only soft recommendations, and concluded that no issue required legal consultation or self-disclosure. Management (Stein, CFO, Narayan) received it.')
B('**Errors in the Manual.** It overstates the substantially-all test (per-physician), lists ASC services as DHS, cites outdated CMP and FCA penalty amounts, and states supervision rules more stringent than Medicare requires, which Greenfield then did not follow.')
H('Analysis', 3)
P('These facts bear on FCA scienter (“reckless disregard” and “deliberate ignorance”) and on the 60-day overpayment rule. Management received specific written notice of the lease-rate variance, the satellite issue and the radiologist issue in March 2022, and hotline notice of the RQB in April 2023. The government can argue that overpayments were “identified,” or should have been through reasonable diligence, long ago. The audit memo is unlikely to be privileged. Under DOJ’s Evaluation of Corporate Compliance Programs and OIG’s November 2023 General Compliance Program Guidance, the program as operated would not earn mitigation credit. Prompt, visible reform is needed both for compliance and for any negotiated resolution.')
H('Remediation', 3)
N('Remove Dr. Stein and Dr. Narayan from the Compliance Committee and from decisions on matters in which they are interested. Have the CCO report to the full Members (or an independent board committee) with direct access to outside counsel. Consider an independent compliance consultant or a monitor-style reviewer.')
N('Re-open hotline matters #2023-07, #2023-11, #2023-13 and #2023-14 under a privileged, counsel-directed investigation (Upjohn protocols).')
N('Hold Compliance Committee meetings at least quarterly, with minutes. Deliver annual Stark/AKS/FCA training (special modules for the Compensation Committee, lease administration, billing and site managers). Complete a counsel-directed risk assessment within 90 days. Revise the Manual to correct the legal errors identified above.')
N('Build an arrangements database (all physician and referral-source contracts, leases and in-kind services) with FMV support, expiration tracking and pre-execution legal and compliance sign-off.')

P('The following discrepancies undermine the reliability of Greenfield’s records and must be reconciled, under privilege, before any disclosure or damages model is built:')
T(['Item', 'Discrepancy', 'Source(s)'], [
 ['Employed physician count', '35 (OA § 3.3; Manual; audit; Compl.) vs. 31 in 2023 Comp. Summary; Specialty Breakdown counts (e.g., Cardiology 14, IM 22) do not match Detail sheet (Cardiology 15, IM 21)', 'OA; Comp. Summary'],
 ['Member ownership', 'Listed Greenfield percentages for 52 members total 98.3%, not 100%', 'Comp. Summary Detail'],
 ['Member profit distributions', 'Line items total \$3,729,100 vs. stated subtotal \$3,814,000 (\$84,900 gap); Stein and Narayan not pro rata', 'Comp. Summary'],
 ['Buckeye ownership', 'Individual members’ Buckeye percentages total 113.5%; Buckeye OA (never amended) shows only Greenfield 60/Stein 25/Narayan 15', 'Comp. Summary; Buckeye OA § 3.1, Ex. A, § 12.2 note'],
 ['Buckeye referred cases', 'Credits computed on all 900 cases attributed to members vs. 702 Greenfield-referred cases alleged; OA “hypothetical” uses 702/342/56', 'Comp. Summary; Compl. ¶ 78; Buckeye OA § 4.1(c)'],
 ['Arithmetic', 'Dr. Banerjee components sum to \$840,954 but total shown is \$841,954', 'Comp. Summary row 4'],
 ['Summary totals', 'Specialty grand total compensation \$54,162,150 vs. category grand total \$58,130,900', 'Comp. Summary, Summary tab'],
 ['RQB effective date', 'Effective Jan. 1, 2022 (memo) vs. Jan. 10, 2022 (audit); RQB language in OA effective Jan. 1, 2020', 'Comp. Memo; audit § V; OA § 7.5(c)'],
 ['Benchmark / appraisal dates', 'Compensation study Nov. 2019; real-estate appraisal Sept. 15, 2020; audit refers to both', 'Audit §§ II, IV'],
 ['Appraisal basis', 'Appraisal is FSG; Pinnacle Ex. B says “triple-net equivalent”', 'Appraisal §§ 1, 7; Pinnacle Ex. B'],
 ['Distribution description', 'Comp. memo and Comp. Summary notes say member distributions are ownership-proportional; OA § 8.4 Referral Credits', 'Comp. Memo § 6; OA § 8.4'],
 ['Execution', 'Signature lines blank on MDA, ClearView and Pinnacle leases, Buckeye OA (file copies)', 'Various'],
 ['Hotline anonymity', 'Relator claims she filed the RQB and lease reports; log records #2023-07 and #2023-14 as anonymous', 'Compl. ¶¶ 40, 96, 98–99; Hotline log'],
], widths=[1.4, 3.6, 1.5], fs=8)

I've written the Stark Law issues memorandum: `/workspace/output/stark-law-issues-memorandum.docx`, about 12,600 words. The docx validator passed and it reads back cleanly with `parse-doc`. I read all 15 source documents in full, including the docx headers and footers and every spreadsheet tab, and did all work through `sbx.sh`.

The memo is dated today. The record only runs to October 2024, and several arrangements have since expired, so the memo says each conclusion needs re-checking against current facts.

The memo has 12 issues, a risk matrix, and a fix plan with a decision on whether to self-disclose. The main findings:

1. **Referral Quality Bonus (Critical).** Employed physicians get $150 per completed internal referral, including to Greenfield's own lab and imaging, capped at $90,000 a year. In 2023, $1,260,000 went to 31 physicians, which is 8,400 paid referrals. That rules out the Stark employment exception for every recipient. Greenfield's March 2022 internal audit and a 2023 hotline report both cleared it without involving the Compliance Committee or outside counsel. The bonus language already appears in the operating agreement dated January 1, 2020, so the look-back may need to start before 2022.
2. **Loss of group-practice status (Critical).** The same bonus very likely means Greenfield no longer qualifies as a "group practice" under § 411.352(g). Without that, the in-office ancillary services exception is gone for all 87 physicians and all in-house lab and imaging billing since January 2022. The whistleblower's complaint does not clearly plead this. It is probably the largest exposure.
3. **Pinnacle lab lease (High).** Rent is $22/sf on terms where the tenant pays only expense increases, against a $28–$32/sf appraisal range that already includes expenses. That puts it $10,800–$18,000 a year below market. The appraisal was about 18 months old when the lease was signed, and the lease exhibit wrongly describes it as "triple-net." The tenant's CEO and the appraiser share the surname Cho; any relationship needs checking.
4. **Free Pinnacle courier (High).** Pinnacle provides about $50,400 a year of courier service to all 12 sites with no written agreement. Whether this is a problem depends on what the courier actually carries.
5. **Buckeye surgery center (Critical under the Anti-Kickback Statute, Medium under Stark).** Profits go out by each owner's referral share, and Greenfield adds a 0.5% "Referral Credit" on each referred case's facility fee. Ownership percentages in the compensation spreadsheet add up to 113.5%.
6. **Dr. Stein's medical directorship (High).** $120,000 a year for 96 hours, about $1,250 an hour, unchanged since 2016, never benchmarked, and approved by conflicted insiders.
7. **Hilliard and Dublin satellites (High).** Lab testing runs daily, but a physician is on site only part of the week, so the "same building" test likely fails.
8. **Contract radiologists (Medium).** The internal audit and compliance manual apply the 75% test to each physician; the rule actually measures group members as a whole. The real risks are the anti-markup rule, reassignment paperwork and where reads are performed.
9. **ClearView lease (Medium).** At $18/sf plus about $12/sf of expenses it is roughly $30/sf, which is inside the appraised range. It is likely defensible, unlike what the audit, a hotline report and the complaint assumed.
10. **Committee pay (Medium).** The only two physicians on the Compensation Committee, Drs. Stein and Narayan, received quality bonuses over the 25% cap ($3,250 and $35,000). Their profit distributions are also off pro rata.
11. **Compliance program (High).** Meetings were skipped, there was no training in 2023–24 and no recent risk assessment, and all three Stark-related hotline reports were closed without escalation.
12. **Records (Medium).** The data has discrepancies: a 35 vs. 31 physician count, profit-distribution totals that don't add up, and arithmetic errors.

The memo also tests the whistleblower's complaint against the documents. Some of its errors help the defense: it says $200 per referral instead of $150, says all 87 physicians were paid, treats surgery-center procedures as Stark-covered services when they are excluded, and overstates the ClearView subsidy. The memo also lists the problems the complaint leaves out, which raise the risk of an amended complaint.
